entries.moment: Thebes during the reign of Hatshepsut, c. 1470 BCE (her architect Senenmut; 'scribes of the fields' re-measuring land with knotted ropes after each Nile flood)

male.outfit: Calf-length wrap-around kilt of fine bleached white linen, knotted at the waist, with the overlapping front edge falling in a slanting, finely pleated panel. Bare torso; plain papyrus or leather sandals. Everything is white or ecru linen, so the bright beadwork at the neck stands out.
male.hair: Official's bobbed wig: straight black wig cut bluntly at shoulder length with a short straight fringe, falling over the ears or tucked behind them (head shaved underneath)
male.facialHair: none (clean-shaven; the false beard was royal and must not be used)
male.headwear: none
male.accessory: Wesekh broad collar: a flat semicircular collar of many rows of faience beads (turquoise, lapis blue, carnelian red, gold) with a row of teardrop pendants on the outer edge, covering the upper chest and shoulders

female.outfit: Ankle-length, close-fitting sheath dress of fine white linen that covers the bust and is held up by two broad shoulder straps; papyrus sandals or barefoot. No overgarment: the sheer pleated over-robes came one or two generations later.
female.hair: Tripartite wig: a long, heavy, straight black wig parted in the centre, with two thick lappets falling in front of the shoulders to the chest and the rest hanging down the back
female.headwear: Thin floral fillet: a narrow band of blue-lotus petals tied round the wig, with a single lotus bud over the forehead
female.accessory: Wesekh broad collar of rows of turquoise, lapis, carnelian and gold faience beads with teardrop pendants

entries.signature: The broad beaded wesekh collar worn over crisp white linen, with a heavy black wig (kohl-winged eyes on the face layer)
avoid: nemes striped headcloth, uraeus cobra, vulture crown, blue khepresh crown (all royal or divine)
false beard, crook and flail
Hollywood 'Cleopatra' styling or gold lame
sheer pleated over-robes, knotted shawls and layered 'duplex' wigs (later 18th-dynasty and Amarna fashion)
perfume/wax cones on the head (banquet-only, and they read as a hat)
Greek draped chiton/himation and fibula brooches (reads as Greece-ancient; Ptolemaic Alexandria was largely Greek-dressed)
coloured or fringed wool wraps and long beards (read as Mesopotamia)
ankh or god emblems as ornaments
mummy wrappings, pyramids or sphinx props
entries.notes: Hatshepsut's Thebes was chosen over Cleopatra's Alexandria because Ptolemaic civilian dress was largely Greek and would blur with Greece-ancient. The look follows early-to-mid 18th-dynasty Theban tomb paintings of officials and scribes (Rekhmire TT100 under Thutmose III; Menna TT69, a 'scribe of the fields' whose tomb shows land surveyors with measuring ropes, is slightly later, c. 1400 BCE) and statues of Senenmut. Men were clean-shaven and wore wigs, and both sexes wore the broad collar. Kohl eyeliner for both sexes goes on the face layer. Correction: the original draft said 'short-sleeved' wig, which is a wrong term. The knotted sheer shawl was removed because sheer pleated overgarments became common only from about Amenhotep II–III onward. Around 1470 BCE the strapped sheath dress was the standard women's garment; it is drawn covering the bust for modesty. The blue lotus fillet comes from banquet scenes and is ornamental, not a cult object.

entries.moment: Babylon under Hammurabi, c. 1760 BCE (the law code, clay contracts sealed with cylinder seals)

male.outfit: Ankle-length wrap of heavy dyed wool (madder red, blue or yellow) wound round the body and thrown over the left shoulder, leaving the right shoulder and arm bare. Every edge has a thick rolled fringe or tufted border, and a wide cloth belt holds it at the waist. Plain leather sandals.
male.hair: Long hair drawn back into a low, rounded chignon (bun) at the nape
male.facialHair: Full, long beard reaching the upper chest, squared at the bottom, combed into long wavy strands that end in neat rows of small curls, with a moustache
male.headwear: Narrow twisted-wool headband (fillet) circling the head and holding the hair
male.accessory: Lapis-lazuli cylinder seal: a finger-length carved stone cylinder hung on a cord around the neck. It was the owner's signature, rolled onto clay contracts.

female.outfit: Ankle-length shawl-dress of dyed wool (saffron-yellow, rust or blue), wound round the body with the end thrown over the left shoulder so the right shoulder is bare. A thick contrasting fringe runs along its edges and spirals down the body in one or two bands. It is a fringed wrap, not a tiered flounced robe.
female.hair: Centre-parted hair braided into one thick plait wound round the head like a crown
female.headwear: A wide gold-thread ribbon wound over the coiled braid, hung with small gold ring pendants
female.accessory: A pair of long bronze toggle pins (tudittum) fastening the shawl at the chest, linked by a looping string of carnelian and lapis beads

entries.signature: The heavily fringed, coloured wool wrap draped over the left shoulder with the right shoulder bare; men also have the long chest-length curled beard and the hair bun
avoid: horned crowns (divine) and Hammurabi's royal brimmed cap
tiered flounced robes (in Old Babylonian art these are goddess dress, e.g. the Lama goddess)
Assyrian winged bulls (lamassu), Ishtar Gate dragons and other religious motifs
Sumerian sheepskin kaunakes skirts (an earlier period)
plain, unfringed Greek-style himation with short hair and a short beard (reads as Greece-ancient)
white linen, broad bead collars, wigs or clean-shaven faces (read as Egypt)
maces, weapons, or clay tablets held in the hand
entries.notes: Sources: the Code of Hammurabi stele in the Louvre (a long robe with a rolled border draped over the left shoulder, a long full beard, hair in a bun), the Mari palace wall paintings (c. 1780 BCE), Old Babylonian terracotta plaques, and the World History Encyclopedia article 'Fashion & Dress in Ancient Mesopotamia' (a fringed shawl over the left shoulder with the right arm free; women's braids wound round the head with ribbons and pendants; fringe and length signalled rank). Correction: the woman's dress was changed from 'several layered bands of fringe', which drifts toward the tiered flounced robe that marks goddesses in Old Babylonian art (a sacred-dress risk), to a single fringed wrap. The beard was changed from strict horizontal rows of tight curls, which is more Neo-Assyrian, to long wavy strands ending in curls, closer to Old Babylonian royal heads. The dye colours are reconstructed from textile terms in the Mari texts and are uncertain. The cylinder seal fits the game's 'records and contracts' theme. The Greek himation also leaves the right shoulder bare, so the thick visible fringe, the chest-length beard and the bun must stay prominent.

entries.moment: Athens in the age of Pericles and Socrates, c. 430 BCE

male.outfit: Short, knee-length wool chiton in undyed cream or saffron, under a large rectangular himation (wool mantle) in a colour such as madder red, blue-grey or saffron. The himation wraps round the body and is thrown over the left shoulder, leaving the right arm and shoulder free (the chiton covers the chest). Its hem has a woven meander (Greek key) border in dark red or black. Simple strapped leather sandals or bare feet.
male.hair: Classical Athenian crop: short-to-medium thick curls brushed forward, half covering the ears
male.facialHair: Full, rounded, neatly trimmed beard with moustache (the norm for an adult Athenian citizen)
male.headwear: Petasos: a flat, wide-brimmed felt traveller's hat with a low crown, worn tilted back on the head with the brim turned up at the front so the face is fully clear, tied under the chin with a thin cord
male.accessory: Pera: a small soft leather traveller's pouch on a thin strap slung diagonally across the body from the left shoulder, over the himation

female.outfit: Ankle-length Ionic chiton of fine crinkled linen, with short sleeves formed by a row of small pins along the upper arms. A himation in saffron, madder red or indigo is wrapped diagonally over one shoulder, with a meander or wave-pattern band at its hem.
female.hair: Centre-parted wavy hair drawn back to a bun at the nape, with a few curls escaping at the temples
female.headwear: Sakkos: a patterned cloth snood that wraps the bun and the back of the head, leaving the forehead and face fully visible
female.accessory: Narrow woven girdle tied at the natural waist, with the chiton bloused over it (kolpos)

entries.signature: The coloured himation with a woven meander (Greek key) border, draped over one shoulder with no curved toga edge; men add a beard and the flat petasos traveller's hat, and women add the patterned sakkos snood
avoid: Roman toga with a curved, rounded edge or a U-shaped front fold, or a tunic with purple stripes (reads as Rome)
clean-shaven adult men (reads as Roman)
laurel or olive victory wreaths
Corinthian helmet from Pericles' busts, hoplite armour, Spartan red cloak (military)
short chlamys cloak pinned at the shoulder with petasos (the ephebe/cadet and hunting costume)
all-white marble-statue clothing (real Greek dress was coloured)
'toga party' bedsheet look
girdle high under the bust (a Hellenistic fashion, a century later)
Greek national flag colours or modern symbols
priestess or temple ritual dress (sacred)
entries.notes: Sources: Attic red-figure and white-ground vase painting, the Parthenon frieze (c. 440 BCE), Lee, 'Body, Dress and Identity in Ancient Greece' (2015), and Llewellyn-Jones, 'Aphrodite's Tortoise' (2003). Changes: the petasos moved from a hat slung behind the shoulders, which is invisible on a front-facing figure and could read as a halo, to being worn on the head. Travellers wear it in vase painting, which fits a time traveller at a border desk. The freed accessory slot became a pera shoulder pouch. The woman's girdle moved from high under the bust (mostly Hellenistic) to the natural waist, normal c. 430 BCE. The sandal term was simplified because krepides were heavier travelling or military footwear. To tell Greece from Italy in this era: beard, coloured himation with a woven border, petasos and sandals (Greece) against a clean-shaven face, a plain white toga with a curved edge, clavus stripe and closed calcei (Rome). Socrates famously wore only a coarse tribon cloak and went barefoot, so a plainer variant is fine. Archimedes (Syracuse, c. 250 BCE) was culturally Greek: dress him in himation and chiton, never a toga. Respectable Athenian women often pulled the himation over the head outdoors; the sakkos is an equally attested, face-clear option.

entries.moment: Rome in the last years of the Republic, under Julius Caesar, c. 50 BCE

male.outfit: Knee-length white wool tunica with two narrow reddish-purple vertical stripes (angusticlavus, associated with the equestrian business class), under a long, ample, plain off-white wool toga. The toga is draped the late-Republican way: over the left shoulder, round the back, under the right arm and back up across the front to the left shoulder, forming a firm diagonal band across the chest. Its distinctive rounded (curved) lower edge hangs to the ankles and dips lower at the sides. The right-hand clavus stripe shows at the right side of the chest. Closed black leather calcei ankle boots with laced straps, not sandals.
male.hair: Late-Republican short crop, cut close and combed forward onto the brow (Caesar style)
male.facialHair: none (clean-shaven, the Roman norm of the period)
male.headwear: none
male.accessory: Gold signet ring (anulus aureus, the equestrian gold ring) on the left hand

female.outfit: A long-sleeved tunica with a sleeveless, floor-length stola over it on narrow shoulder straps (the dress of a respectable married woman). A large plain rectangular palla (mantle) with no patterned border is draped over the left shoulder and around the body. Ochre, rose, sea-green or blue wool, not purple.
female.hair: Nodus hairstyle: a raised roll of hair pushed up and pinned above the forehead, the sides waved back, the rest braided into a small bun at the nape
female.headwear: none
female.accessory: Gold earrings with pearl drops (crotalia)

entries.signature: Men: a plain white toga with a curved, rounded edge over a tunic with a narrow purple clavus stripe, worn clean-shaven with calcei boots. Women: the nodus roll of hair above the forehead, with the strapped stola.
avoid: deep knee-length sinus fold and chest pouch (umbo): these are Augustan (umbo from c. 10 BCE), a generation too late
laurel wreath (triumphal or imperial)
toga praetexta or all-purple toga (magistrate or emperor)
broad senatorial stripe (latus clavus)
legionary armour, red military cloak, gladiator gear
beards on men (reads as Greek or later imperial)
Greek-key or other patterned borders (keep those for Greece)
sandals worn with the toga
Vestal or priestly veiling, toga drawn over the head (sacred)
arm held in a toga sling (a statue pose that fights the layered body rig)
entries.notes: Sources: Sebesta & Bonfante (eds.), 'The World of Roman Costume' (1994); Rothfus, 'The Gens Togata: Changing Styles and Changing Identities' (AJP 2010, after Goette 1990); the Via Statilia funerary relief and late-Republican togati; and the Tusculum Caesar portrait. Correction: the draft's U-shaped sinus with an umbo pouch is Augustan. Rothfus and Goette date the sinus to the late 1st century BCE–Augustan period and the umbo to around the Ara Pacis (9 BCE), so the Ara Pacis is not a model for 50 BCE. In Caesar's day the toga had become long (ankle-length 'like a Greek pallium') and full, but was still a single-layer drape. Its curved edge was what told a Roman apart from a Greek in the pallium even then, so the curved hem, the plain white colour, the visible clavus, the clean-shaven face and the calcei now carry the tell. Statues often show the right arm in a toga 'sling'; for drawing, the arm is left free, which the Arringatore-type drape also allowed. The toga was formal civic dress, and travellers often wore a hooded paenula instead, but the toga is the clearest tell against Greece. The anulus aureus was loosely rather than strictly equestrian in the Republic. The nodus is best attested in the 40s–30s BCE (Fulvia and Octavia coin portraits), so it is slightly forward-dated for c. 50 BCE; a simple centre-parted nape bun is the conservative fallback. Suetonius records Caesar buying Servilia a costly pearl, and pearls were a Roman status craze.

entries.moment: Luoyang, the Eastern Han capital, c. 105 CE, when Cai Lun presented his improved paper to the court

male.outfit: Ankle-length, straight-hemmed wrap robe (zhiju paofu) closed with the wearer's left panel over the right, making a 'y' at the throat, with two or three layered collars (the innermost white). The sleeves are huge, bagging out below the arm and narrowing at the wrist. The ground is black, deep red or brown silk with broad contrasting patterned borders at collar, cuffs and hem, tied at the waist with a cloth sash on a small bronze belt hook. Black cloth shoes with upturned square toes peek from the hem.
male.hair: Han topknot (fa ji): all hair combed smoothly up from forehead and nape into a single knot on the crown, no fringe
male.facialHair: Thin moustache with slightly upturned tips and a short pointed chin beard
male.headwear: Jieze: a close-fitting black cloth cap with a stiff band across the forehead, a raised roof-shaped ridge on top covering the topknot, and two short upright flaps ('ears') standing at the back. No chin ties.
male.accessory: Zanbi: a slim bamboo writing brush tucked upright into the side of the cap, as Han scribes kept brushes in the hair or cap

female.outfit: Floor-length quju shenyi: a wrap robe whose long curved front panel spirals round the body, making layered diagonal bands on the skirt. Wide drooping sleeves narrow at the wrist, and two or three cross-collars layer at the neck, the wearer's left over right. Deep red, black or ochre silk with checked or cloud-scroll borders, cinched with a sash. The silhouette is narrow and trails at the hem.
female.hair: Chuishao ji: centre-parted hair drawn smoothly back into a low looped bun at the nape, with a short tail of hair hanging below it
female.headwear: none
female.accessory: Jade bi-disc pendant hanging from the sash on a red silk cord with a tassel

entries.signature: A floor-length cross-collar wrap robe with huge bag-shaped 'ox-dewlap' sleeves and broad dark borders; men add the roof-ridged black jieze cap
avoid: Emperor's mianguan crown with bead curtains, dragon robes or imperial yellow
jinxian guan ridged official hat or coloured seal-ribbons (shou), which mark rank
armour, swords, crossbows
Qing items (queue braid, skullcap, horse-hoof cuffs) or Tang/Ming items
Japanese elements: mizura side loops, magatama beads, short jacket with trousers tied at the knee
conical 'coolie' straw hat, Fu Manchu moustache, any slanted-eye caricature
robe closed with the right panel over the left (reversed)
chin ties on the jieze (ties belong to the formal guan hat worn on top of it)
entries.notes: Sources: Mawangdui Tomb 1 silks and figurines (Western Han, c. 168 BCE); Eastern Han tomb figurines, reliefs and murals (Wu Liang shrines, Holingol, Dahuting); Book of Later Han, 'Treatise on Carriages and Clothing', for the ze and jinxian guan. Correction: the jieze was a band cap (a forehead band called yanti, two upright 'ears' at the back and a roof-like top) and had no chin ribbons. The ties were for the formal guan worn over it, which is left out because its ridges mark official rank. By Eastern Han the ze was worn across social classes, and the roof-topped jieze was the civil (non-military) form. Men's curved-hem robes had largely given way to straight hems (zhiju) by Eastern Han, but women's quju robes continued through Eastern Han into Wei-Jin, so the spiral hem is kept for the woman. Mawangdui is about 270 years earlier, so treat the border patterns as indicative. Cai Lun was a palace eunuch official, so draw a generic Han scribe rather than him. If the brush reads as a plain hairpin at sprite size, swap the accessory for a bronze belt hook with a hanging jade.

entries.moment: Yamato (the Nara–Osaka plain) in the Kofun period, c. 450 CE, the age of the great keyhole tombs and haniwa clay figures

male.outfit: Kinu: a hip-length jacket of undyed white hemp with narrow tube sleeves, fastened at the chest with two small cloth bows and belted at the waist. Loose white hakama trousers are gathered and tied just below each knee with cords (ashi-yui), so they balloon above. Bare feet or simple straw sandals; optional simple red triangle or dot trim.
male.hair: Mizura: hair parted in the centre, with each side looped into a figure-eight bundle tied beside the ears and hanging to the jaw
male.facialHair: none
male.headwear: none
male.accessory: Necklace of green jade magatama (comma-shaped beads) strung with cylindrical kudatama beads

female.outfit: White hemp kinu jacket with narrow sleeves, fastened with small cloth bows and belted at the waist, over a mo: a long wrapped skirt to the ankle, sometimes pleated or striped in red and white.
female.hair: Flat 'board' chignon: hair gathered on top of the head into a long, flat bun lying front to back, tied at its middle, with a small comb at the front
female.headwear: none
female.accessory: Multi-strand necklace of green magatama and round blue glass beads

entries.signature: A short belted jacket over knee-tied trousers or a long skirt, with a big green comma-shaped magatama bead necklace; men also wear mizura hair loops beside the ears (the clearest silhouette cue), and women the flat board chignon
avoid: keiko armour, swords, helmets (the famous haniwa warrior)
shrine-maiden ritual sash (osuhi), bronze mirrors, anything liturgical
a single oversized jewel styled as the imperial regalia
red face paint seen on haniwa (reads as war paint or caricature)
later kimono with a wide obi, or Heian court robes
Chinese long robes with huge sleeves, or topknot caps
entries.notes: Sources: haniwa figures in the Tokyo National Museum and elsewhere (a seated man with mizura; a woman with a flat hair bun and bead necklaces; jackets tied with bows at the chest); Wei Zhi 'Account of the Wa' (3rd c.) for the earlier Yayoi look. Correction: the rule that robes close with the left panel over the right, as in China, came from an edict of 719 CE (Yoro 3, Shoku Nihongi: 'first ordered the common people to wear the right lapel'), not the 718 Yoro Code. Before it, haniwa show the closure both ways, so closure direction was dropped as a tell and the jacket is described as fastened with bows. Japan is instead told apart from Han China by the short jacket with knee-tied trousers or a skirt, the mizura or flat chignon, and the magatama. None of the designer's figures falls in this era. Magatama also occur in Korea, but Korea is not a game nation.

entries.moment: Camulodunum (Colchester), the trading capital of the Catuvellauni under Cunobelinus, c. 20 CE: shortly before the Roman conquest, while wine and luxury goods were arriving from Roman Gaul

male.outfit: Knee-length belted wool tunic over close-fitting trousers (bracae), both woven in bold multicoloured checks of red, mustard yellow and green. A thick, short rectangular cloak in a contrasting check is pinned at the right shoulder. Soft leather ankle shoes.
male.hair: Long swept-back mane: shoulder-length hair brushed straight back off the forehead, thick and full
male.facialHair: Long drooping moustache that hangs past the corners of the mouth; chin and cheeks clean-shaven
male.headwear: none
male.accessory: Twisted gold torc: a thick, rope-twisted open neck ring with rounded knob ends meeting at the throat

female.outfit: Ankle-length, long-sleeved tunic-dress of bright checked wool in red, yellow and green, cinched with a woven belt. Over it hangs a thick, plain dark-red or ochre wool mantle, fastened at the chest with a bronze brooch enamelled in red with swirling La Tene curves.
female.hair: Very long centre-parted hair in two thick braids falling to the waist
female.headwear: none
female.accessory: Twisted gold or bronze torc at the neck

entries.signature: The rope-twisted gold torc at the throat, worn with bold multicoloured checked wool
avoid: blue woad body paint or tattoos (skin must never carry the signal)
horned or winged helmets
Roman toga, tunic-with-toga or Roman armour
swords, shields, spears, chariot-warrior gear
Scottish kilts or clan tartans (anachronistic by 1,500+ years)
Suebian side-knot hairstyle or full beard (that is Germany-ancient)
plain undyed or single-colour cloth with amber beads (reads as Germany-ancient)
fur-loincloth 'savage barbarian' caricature
druid robes or any religious costume
entries.notes: Sources: Caesar, Gallic War 5.14 (Britons wore their hair long and shaved everything except the head and upper lip, hence the moustache with a bare chin); Cassius Dio 62.2 (Boudica in a multicoloured tunic, a thick mantle fastened with a brooch and a great gold torc, with very long hair); Diodorus 5.30 (Celtic cloaks woven in close multicoloured checks; hair drawn back from the forehead). The Snettisham Great Torc (c. 75 BCE) and La Tene enamelled brooches are the models for the jewellery. No changes to substance; the entry checks out. Uncertain: no British Iron Age garments survive intact, so cut and colour are reconstructed from Gaulish and continental parallels and classical descriptions. The braids are a reasonable choice, but Dio describes loose hair. Camulodunum fits Britain's trade-network theme. Against Germany-ancient, the checks, the torc and the moustache-only face must stay prominent, because both nations share the tunic, trousers and cloak silhouette.

entries.moment: Free Germania east of the Rhine and north of the Danube, c. 98 CE, as described in Tacitus' Germania

male.outfit: Tight-fitting, long-sleeved, knee-length wool tunic and close-fitting long trousers, as in the Thorsberg bog finds, in undyed brown and deep woad blue with a diamond-twill texture. A short, dark rectangular wool cloak with a fringed, tablet-woven border is pinned at the right shoulder. Leather wrap shoes.
male.hair: Suebian knot: hair combed back and to the side and twisted into a tight knot on the right side of the head, above the temple
male.facialHair: Full short beard
male.headwear: none
male.accessory: Bronze bow brooch (eye-fibula) pinning the cloak at the right shoulder

female.outfit: Loose, sleeveless, ankle-length linen tube dress (peplos type) pinned at each shoulder with a small bronze brooch, leaving the arms bare, with red-purple bands at the neck and hem as Tacitus notes. A plain undyed wool shawl drapes round the shoulders, and the waist is tied with a woven band. Draw it modestly: fuller and draped, not a fitted sheath.
female.hair: Long hair gathered into a low knot at the nape, bound with a narrow woven wool hair-band wound round it
female.headwear: none
female.accessory: Necklace of chunky orange Baltic amber and glass beads

entries.signature: For men, the Suebian side-knot hairstyle with a full beard. For women, a chunky Baltic amber necklace over a sleeveless, shoulder-pinned linen dress with red-purple trim.
avoid: horned or winged helmets
Viking or Wagnerian-opera stereotypes
fur trims, pelts or fur-loincloth barbarian caricature
spears, shields or any weapons; Roman armour
gold torc or bright multicoloured checks (that is Britain-ancient)
fitted white strapped sheath dress or broad bead collar (reads as Egypt-ancient)
snood or hairnet over the bun (too close to the Greek sakkos)
Viking-age oval brooches with bead strings between them (the wrong period)
Roman toga or Roman-style jewellery
entries.notes: Sources: Tacitus, Germania 17 (a short cloak fastened with a clasp; wealthy men in tight garments that follow each limb; women in linen trimmed with purple, without sleeves, arms bare) and Germania 38 (the Suebian knot). The Osterby head (Schleswig-Holstein) preserves an actual Suebian knot on the right side. The Thorsberg finds (trousers, tunic, fringed cloak) date to the 2nd-3rd century CE, slightly later than this moment. Changes: the fur collar was removed from the man's cloak. Tacitus mentions pelts, but fur pushes the figure toward the barbarian caricature and Thorsberg shows fringed wool. The woman's sprang hairnet was removed: it is only weakly attested for 1st-century Germania (the secure finds are Danish Bronze Age and some Iron Age bog finds), and at thumbnail size it duplicates the Greek sakkos. She now has a woven hair-band like the one on the Huldremose woman. The dress is now a loose peplos-type dress pinned at both shoulders, to separate it from the Egyptian sheath. Baltic amber was the region's main trade good. Beards follow Roman depictions of Germanic men, such as the Marcus Aurelius column.

entries.moment: Mamluk Cairo under al-Nasir Muhammad, c. 1340 CE (the al-Khalij al-Nasiri canal was dug in 1325 and the Nile flood was read at the Roda Nilometer)

male.outfit: Ankle-length pale linen qamis under an open, front-opening farajiyya, the long outer robe of Mamluk scholars, judges and scribes. The farajiyya is deep green, brown or dark blue wool (never black), with very wide, long sleeves that fall well past the fingertips because ample sleeves marked civilian status. No embroidered armbands. Soft leather boots.
male.hair: Short-cropped, hidden under the turban
male.facialHair: Full, rounded, neatly trimmed beard with a moustache
male.headwear: Large, broad, rounded white muslin turban ('imama) wound low and full around a small hidden cap, with no cap showing above it. One loose end (the 'adhaba tail) hangs behind one shoulder.
male.accessory: Broad woven-silk girdle wound at the waist, with long knotted fringe ends

female.outfit: Ankle-length silk qamis in saffron, crimson or emerald with small woven motifs. It has very wide sleeves that hang well below the hands and is worn over full trousers (sirwal) gathered at the ankle. Over it, a large plain WHITE linen izar is draped from the head down to the ankles and hangs open at the front, so a strip of the bright qamis and its big sleeves shows down the middle.
female.hair: Long hair braided and hidden under the izar, with only a thin edge of hair at the brow
female.headwear: The top of the white izar drawn over the head as a soft hood that frames the fully visible face, with no face veil
female.accessory: Gold filigree collar necklace with small hanging pendants

entries.signature: Men: a big, low, round white turban with a hanging tail, worn with very long, wide sleeves. Women: a full-length white izar hooded over the head and hanging open over a brightly coloured gown.
avoid: Mamluk military dress: kallawta cap, heraldic blazons or roundels, metal-plaque belts, swords, bows
Abbasid tall black qalansuwa cap, black robes, tiraz script armbands, or taylasan/tarha shawl over the shoulders (read as Iraq-medieval)
Blue, yellow or red izars, or any colour-coded turban: these colours were imposed on Christian, Jewish and Samaritan subjects
face-covering veils (burqu')
Ottoman tall kavuk turbans
the tall tartur/taqiyya women's caps (15th century and later, and banned in 1426/7)
harem or belly-dance cliches
Crusader imagery
entries.notes: Sources: lugatism.com, 'Outer garments' and 'Headwear' in the Mamluk Sultanate. These say the farajiyya was the long-sleeved robe of the learned class and could carry tiraz bands, which are dropped here so it does not echo Iraq. They also say women's izars were typically white for Muslim women, while blue, yellow and red were the colours imposed on Christian, Jewish and Samaritan women, which is why the izar must stay white. Rawi, 'Turbans and Textiles', describes the izar as a large rectangle draped over head and shoulders, long sleeves as normal, and turbans as major status spending. Parani and Stillman (Arab Dress, p. 65) note that in the Mamluk state longer sleeves meant higher status. Removed: the claim that sultans issued decrees shortening women's sleeves. I could not verify it; the decrees I found (1426/7 and 1472) concern women's caps. Blue-and-white checked izar fragments from Quseir al-Qadim were considered and rejected because the blue could read as the colour imposed on Christians. The traveller is a civilian 'man of the pen' in the irrigation or land-survey office. The 'adhaba tail is a scholarly habit and optional.

entries.moment: Baghdad under the Abbasids, c. 830 CE (al-Khwarizmi at the House of Wisdom; translation and algebra)

male.outfit: Ankle-length pale linen qamis and sirwal under a front-opening, calf-length durra'a robe of black wool or silk. Bands of gold-embroidered decorative Arabic-style pseudo-script (tiraz) circle both upper sleeves. The sleeves are moderately wide and end at the wrist. Soft leather khuff boots.
male.hair: Hair to the nape, mostly hidden under the cap and turban
male.facialHair: Full beard, neatly trimmed and rounded, with a moustache
male.headwear: Qalansuwa tawila: a tall, stiff, smooth black cap (a cone or high cylinder about one and a half times the height of the head) with a white turban wound round its base. The tall black top rises clearly above the turban and stays upright, not soft or crumpled.
male.accessory: Taylasan: a dark shawl draped over the shoulders and hanging down the back like a thrown-back hood, the mark of a scholar

female.outfit: Long-sleeved, ankle-length qamis in a rich colour (rose, saffron or pistachio) with tiraz script bands at the upper arms, over full sirwal gathered at the ankle. A light mantle (rida') lies over the shoulders only, not over the head.
female.hair: Long hair mostly under the veil, with two glossy S-shaped side-curls (sudgh) combed forward onto the cheeks at the temples
female.headwear: Light, sheer khimar veil over the hair, bound at the brow by an 'isaba: a narrow jewelled and embroidered headband carrying a line of decorative pseudo-script
female.accessory: Choker of large pearls

entries.signature: Men: the tall, stiff black qalansuwa cap rising out of a white turban, with tiraz armbands. Women: the jewelled 'isaba band across the brow, with S-shaped side-curls on the cheeks.
avoid: 'Arabian Nights' or Aladdin cliches: curled-toe slippers, genie trousers, onion domes
harem stereotypes and face-covering veils
readable Qur'anic text on clothing (use decorative pseudo-script)
keffiyeh with agal (a later style)
Ottoman bulbous turbans
Mamluk very long hanging sleeves, a big round all-white turban, or a full-length white izar wrap (read as Egypt-medieval)
soft, crumpled or forward-leaning cap (reads as the Japanese eboshi)
Sasanian royal crowns, black battle banners, weapons
entries.notes: The entry was sound and I kept it almost unchanged. Sources: abbasidstudies.org (Clothing); lugatism.com on Abbasid headwear and outer garments (the qalansuwa tawila was a court and scholarly cap with a turban wound round it, and the taylasan was a shawl over the shoulders); Wikipedia, 'Durra'ah'; Encyclopedia.com, 'Middle East: History of Islamic Dress'. The women's side-curls come from the Samarra Jawsaq wall paintings (c. 836), and the jewelled 'isaba is traditionally credited to 'Ulayya bint al-Mahdi. Al-Mansur introduced the tall qalansuwa c. 770, and it was shortened only under al-Musta'in in the 860s, so it is correct for 830. Black was the Abbasid court colour, which suits a scholar at court. I tightened the cap wording (stiff, smooth, upright) so it cannot read as Japan's soft black eboshi, and kept the sleeves at wrist length so they do not echo Egypt. 'Isaba headbands were also worn in Mamluk Egypt, so Egypt's women are given the izar hood instead.

entries.moment: Mystras, capital of the Byzantine Despotate of the Morea, in the circle of the philosopher Gemistos Plethon, c. 1430

male.outfit: Ankle-length kabbadion: a caftan-like robe closed down the centre front with a long row of small round buttons, with long narrow sleeves, in deep green, wine or blue silk with a small woven pattern. No overcoat, so the button row stays fully visible. Soft dark boots.
male.hair: Long hair, centre-parted, falling to the shoulders
male.facialHair: Long full beard with moustache (the Byzantine lay norm, noted by Italian observers in 1438)
male.headwear: Tall felt hat with a high rounded crown and a brim turned sharply up all round against it, with a light crown and a darker brim, as Pisanello sketched among the Byzantine delegation. It must not be the emperor's pointed-visor version, an official's skaranikon with a portrait, or a black clerical kalimavkion.
male.accessory: Belt with small gilt metal mounts, worn at the waist over the kabbadion

female.outfit: A fitted, sleeveless over-dress of patterned silk damask (for example wine red with a small floral pattern), shaped close at the bust and flaring from just below it to the floor, with braided gold trim at the neckline and armholes. Under it is a long T-shaped under-tunic of lighter patterned silk whose long, fitted sleeves show full-length on the arms.
female.hair: Hair fully covered by the headdress; only a smooth edge shows at the forehead
female.headwear: Turban-style headdress (fakiolion): a long strip of cream silk woven with bands of gold and red, wound high and rounded around the head so it covers all the hair. The neck, ears and face stay open, with no cloth wrapped under the chin.
female.accessory: Large gold crescent-shaped (lunate) earrings edged with pearls, hanging clearly below the headdress

entries.signature: Men: a tall felt hat with a high rounded crown and turned-up brim, a long beard and a button-front robe. Women: a compact, patterned, wound turban-headdress with big crescent earrings, over a fitted sleeveless damask over-dress.
avoid: imperial regalia: loros, crowns, purple silk, double-headed eagle
emperor's pointed-visor hat (royalty) and the skaranikon official cap bearing the emperor's portrait (regime insignia)
Orthodox clerical or monastic robes, black kalimavkion, crosses or icons (sacred)
Virgin Mary (Theotokos) style dark star-marked maphorion veil (sacred)
plain white headcloth wrapped round the neck and chin (reads as the Britain headrail) or a full-length white wrap (reads Egypt)
wide bell-sleeved overgown (reads Britain)
the Byzantine 'head donut' padded ring (unattested, and reads as Italy's ghirlanda)
Ottoman white turban on men (anachronistic here; reads Egypt or Iraq)
Italian cappuccio hood-hat, or clean-shaven men (reads Italy)
armour or weapons, including the sabre in Pisanello's sketches
entries.notes: Men: Pisanello's drawings of the Byzantine delegation at Ferrara-Florence (1438) and Gozzoli's Magi Chapel (1459). Parani, 'Cultural Identity and Dress: Byzantine Ceremonial Costume', documents the Late Byzantine kabbadion caftan with a button front and a belt with metal attachments (Kastoria donor, c. 1180), the brimmed skiadion hat, and the skaranikon cap bearing imperial portraits, which is avoided as regime insignia. I dropped the hanging-sleeve overcoat because it hid the button row and echoed Egypt's long sleeves. Women: the old bell-sleeved gown with a white wound headcloth was too close to Britain's headrail and Egypt's white izar at thumbnail size. The new over-dress follows the 15th-century silk damask dress excavated at Mystras (FIT Fashion History Timeline): sleeveless, fitted and flaring from below the bust, with braided trim, over a T-shaped patterned under-tunic. A Mystras donor mural also shows under-layers visible at the bust and sleeves. The wound turban (fakiolion/phakeolion) is attested for Byzantine women (archaeology.wiki; annasrome.com, on the Menologion of Basil II and on grammata bands). Uncertain: the exact 1430 form and colours of women's headdresses. Mystras donor portraits also show plain white headcloths, which were rejected for distinctiveness. Lunate earrings are a slightly archaic choice.

entries.moment: Florence of the Medici bank, during the Council of Florence, 1439

male.outfit: Ankle-length lucco, the Florentine citizen's gown, in deep red (rosato or cremisi) wool. It is closed high at the neck with a small standing collar, falls in straight organ-pipe pleats, is fur-lined, has wide open sleeves and is belted with a narrow leather belt. A dark doublet and hose are worn beneath, with soft black shoes.
male.hair: Early-15th-century Florentine crop: short, rounded, cut above the ears
male.facialHair: none (clean-shaven, the Florentine norm)
male.headwear: Cappuccio a mazzocchio: a padded ring sitting on top of the head like a hat, with draped cloth (foggia) falling to one side and a long band (becchetto) hanging over one shoulder, in red or black. Hair shows below the ring, and it does not enclose the neck like a hood.
male.accessory: Scarsella: a leather merchant's purse hanging from the belt at the hip

female.outfit: Fitted gamurra gown in plain silk with long, close sleeves, under a giornea: an open-sided, sleeveless overgown of crimson or green silk velvet with the Italian pomegranate pattern, falling from the shoulders to the floor with a short train, edged with fur or brocade at the neck. No trailing sleeves.
female.hair: Fashionably plucked high forehead; hair drawn back smoothly and gathered into a coil at the back of the head, partly visible
female.headwear: Ghirlanda: a thick padded roll, like a fat wreath, covered in crimson silk and studded with pearls, set around the crown of the head. No veil, so the drawn-back hair and the high bare forehead show.
female.accessory: Gold brooch (fermaglio) with a pearl cluster, pinned at the neckline

entries.signature: Men: the cappuccio a mazzocchio (a padded ring-hat with a draped side and a long hanging becchetto) with an ankle-length red lucco. Women: the pearl-studded padded ghirlanda roll over bare, drawn-back hair and a plucked high forehead.
avoid: beards on men (reads Byzantine Greek)
tall brimmed Byzantine hat
women's veils, wimples or wound headcloths (read Byzantine, Egypt, Britain or Germany)
floor-trailing hanging sleeves (reads Egypt-medieval)
a hood enclosing the head and neck with a scalloped shoulder cape (reads Germany's Gugel)
cardinal's red galero hat, clerical or papal robes (sacred)
laurel wreath and red-cap 'Dante' costume cliches
the later balzo headdress (1450s-80s, Ferrara and Milan)
condottiere armour or weapons
slashed Renaissance sleeves (too late; reserve for early modern)
Medici family crest or balls emblem
entries.notes: Sources: Masaccio and Masolino, Brancacci Chapel (1420s); Fra Angelico; Pisanello; Fra Filippo Lippi, 'Portrait of a Woman with a Man at a Casement' (c. 1440, Met); Carole Collier Frick, 'Dressing Renaissance Florence' (2002); Florentine sumptuary laws; FIT Fashion History Timeline for 1440-49 (Italian women in gamurra and giornea, with the ghirlanda as the Italian padded roll or bourrelet). Changes: the woman's gauzy white veil became the ghirlanda, because the veil was one of five near-identical pale head coverings in this era. The mazzocchio and the ghirlanda also make padded rolls a family resemblance for Florence. The trailing fur-lined cioppa sleeves became a giornea because they clashed with Egypt's sleeve signature. I dropped 'nape shaved high' from the men's hair because it is a Burgundian and English trait. 1439 is the year the Greek and Italian delegates met, so the neighbour contrast is documented: the Italians were clean-shaven with hood-hats, the Byzantines bearded with tall hats. The mazzocchio descends from the same hood as Germany's Gugel, so its drawing must show it as a ring on top of the head.

entries.moment: Kaifeng, the Northern Song capital, c. 1075. This is the era of Shen Kuo, scholar-official and envoy to the Liao, and of the magnetic compass and movable type.

male.outfit: Ankle-length round-collared robe (yuanling pao) fastened at the right shoulder, with a white inner collar edge at the throat, moderately wide sleeves and a horizontal seam band (lan) across the knees. Plain, unpatterned silk in muted green or blue-grey, the colours of middle-ranking civil officials, not the purple or vermilion of high ranks. Black cloth boots; a long, straight, sober silhouette.
male.hair: Topknot on the crown, fully hidden under the cap; neat hairline
male.facialHair: Long thin moustache and a tapered chin beard, the groomed Song scholar look
male.headwear: Zhijiao futou: a black lacquered-gauze cap with two stiff, straight, flat wings sticking out horizontally from the back. Keep each wing about shoulder-width so the silhouette reads as a 'T'.
male.accessory: Black leather belt worn loose at the hips, set with plain square plaques of black horn or silver

female.outfit: Beizi: a long, straight, open-front coat to mid-calf. Its parallel front edges do not overlap and are edged with a narrow contrasting band; it has high side slits and narrow sleeves. It is worn over a moxiong chest wrap and a long pleated skirt, in pale, understated Song colours: celadon green, ivory, pale pink or light blue.
female.hair: Gaoji: a tall bun piled high on the crown in one or two upright loops, with a few small flower pins
female.headwear: Guanshu: a large arched crescent comb of ivory or lacquer, set upright across the front of the high bun
female.accessory: Pearl drop earrings

entries.signature: Men: the black futou cap with long, stiff, horizontal wings. Women: the tall bun crowned by a big upright crescent comb.
avoid: Ming or Qing items: queue, skullcap, standing collars with metal buttons
official fish pouch (yudai), purple or vermilion high-rank robes, and jade rank belts
emperor's yellow robe, dragons
armour or weapons
Mongol/Yuan-style dress
Japanese eboshi or hitatare
coolie hat or any facial caricature
collar closed right-over-left (zuoren)
futou wings so long they break the sprite frame
entries.notes: The entry was sound and I kept it almost unchanged. Sources: Zhang Zeduan, 'Along the River During the Qingming Festival' (early 12th c.); Song imperial and scholar portraits for the futou and round-collar robe; the Huang Sheng tomb (1243) for the beizi and pleated skirts; Song texts and edicts on high buns and crown combs (the court regulated guanshu size in the mid-11th century, which confirms the fashion). Fixes: the Song 'lanshan' was strictly the pale scholar-student robe, so a coloured robe is correctly the round-collared official robe (yuanling pao), in green or blue-grey, the mid-rank colours. Jade belt plaques marked high rank, so they became horn or silver. Shen Kuo's embassy to the Liao in 1075 makes him a fitting 'diplomat'. The straight-winged futou was the civil official's cap, not a military one. Wing length is shortened for gameplay; real wings could be far longer.

entries.moment: Kyoto under the Ashikaga shogunate, c. 1400: Kitayama culture, Noh theatre, and Japanese folding fans exported to Ming China

male.outfit: Hitatare of hemp: a cross-collared jacket, closed left-over-right, with very wide square sleeves whose cuffs are gathered by a threaded cord. It is tucked into matching ankle-length pleated hakama, with small decorative cord tufts (kikutoji) on the seams and chest ties. Persimmon brown, indigo or olive, with no family crests.
male.hair: Motodori topknot at the crown under a full head of hair (no shaved pate), hidden under the cap
male.facialHair: Short moustache and a small chin tuft
male.headwear: Momi-eboshi: a tall, soft cap of black, lightly lacquered gauze or paper, crumpled and leaning slightly forward
male.accessory: Folding fan (sensu) with black lacquered ribs, closed and tucked into the waist ties at the front

female.outfit: Tsubo-shozoku travel dress: an ankle-length patterned kosode, closed left-over-right, under an outer robe hitched up at the hips so its hem ends at mid-calf, tied with a narrow cloth sash. Muted tie-dyed or small-motif patterns in indigo, rust and cream.
female.hair: Long centre-parted hair worn down, tied once loosely at the nape and falling to the waist
female.headwear: Ichime-gasa: a wide-brimmed lacquered sedge hat with a tall knob crown, worn WITHOUT its veil so the face is fully visible
female.accessory: Small tie-dyed drawstring purse (kinchaku) hanging from the sash

entries.signature: Men: a tall, soft, crumpled black eboshi cap with a wide-sleeved hitatare and hakama. Women: the wide, knob-crowned ichime-gasa travel hat.
avoid: armour, katana, samurai helmets, ninja imagery
Heian junihitoe or court robes (aristocratic and the wrong period)
Buddhist monk kesa or yamabushi robes (liturgical)
amulet pendants (kake-mamori), which are religious
family crests (kamon) on the suo, which can read as a warrior retainer
wide Edo obi or geisha look (anachronistic)
Chinese futou with horizontal wings
a stiff, smooth, upright cap with a turban at its base (reads Iraq's qalansuwa)
collar closed right-over-left (the burial style)
the hanging veil (mushi-no-tareginu) that hides the face
entries.notes: The entry was sound, with minor fixes. The momi-eboshi is the soft, crumpled type; stiff, heavily lacquered caps are the tate-eboshi, so 'lacquered paper' became 'lightly lacquered'. 'Commoner's hemp suo' conflated two garments and became 'hitatare of hemp'. I made the collar direction explicit on both garments. Sources: emaki handscrolls (Ippen Hijiri-e, 1299; Kasuga Gongen Genki-e, 1309) and Muromachi genre paintings. The hitatare was general wear across classes by the Muromachi period. Uncertainty: the tsubo-shozoku is best documented for the Heian and Kamakura periods but persists in pilgrim and traveller imagery. The kinchaku pouch is usually dated from the Muromachi period on and became common later. The eboshi's tall, soft, forward-leaning shape contrasts with the Song futou's horizontal wings and with Iraq's stiff black cone in a white turban.

entries.moment: London under Edward the Confessor, c. 1050: a North Sea port trading wool and silver, where laws of the time mention merchants from Flanders, Normandy and the German Empire

male.outfit: Knee-length wool tunic (cyrtel) in madder red or woad blue, loosely bloused over a belt, with contrasting embroidered or tablet-woven bands at the neckline, cuffs and hem. Loose trousers are wrapped from ankle to knee with linen leg bindings (winingas). A plain rectangular wool cloak is draped over the left shoulder and pinned at the right.
male.hair: Neck-length straight hair, centre-parted and cut evenly at the collar
male.facialHair: Long full moustache with a clean-shaven chin (the English look on the Bayeux Tapestry)
male.headwear: none
male.accessory: Round silver disc brooch with interlace and niello decoration, pinning the cloak at the right shoulder

female.outfit: Ankle-length undergown with tight long sleeves, under a slightly shorter overgown with wide bell sleeves, in soft red, blue or green wool with embroidered cuff bands. A plain mantle hangs from the shoulders.
female.hair: Long hair coiled low at the nape, hidden under the headrail
female.headwear: Headrail: a long rectangular veil of COLOURED wool or linen (blue, brown-red or ochre, contrasting with the gown) laid over the head, wrapped once around the throat and draped down over the shoulders and back. It frames the face but never covers it.
female.accessory: Small round gilt disc brooch closing the mantle at the throat

entries.signature: Men: bareheaded, in the only knee-length tunic of the era, with leg bindings, a cloak pinned at the right shoulder by a round silver disc brooch, and the long English moustache. Women: a coloured headrail veil wrapped over the head and round the throat, above a bell-sleeved overgown.
avoid: horned or winged helmets and Viking-raider stereotypes
chainmail, Norman kite shields, any armour or weapons
crowns or royal regalia
monks' habits, nuns' wimples or any liturgical vestment
white headrail (reads Egypt's white izar and Germany's Kruseler at thumbnail size)
a compact wound turban-headdress (reads Greece)
hood with a long tail (Gugel) or long pointed shoes (Germany-medieval)
frilled Kruseler veil (Germany-medieval)
tall conical hennin or later Gothic headdresses
Robin Hood-style feathered cap and Lincoln green
entries.notes: Sources: the Bayeux Tapestry (1070s), where the English have moustaches and the Normans are clean-shaven; late Anglo-Saxon manuscript illustrations (the Old English Hexateuch, Cotton Claudius B.iv; the Cotton Tiberius B.v calendar; Junius 11), where women's headrails appear in colours; Gale Owen-Crocker, 'Dress in Anglo-Saxon England', for the headrail, leg bindings and gown with overgown; law code IV Aethelred for foreign traders in London. Change: the headrail is now explicitly coloured, because a white one was one of five pale female head coverings in this era. Its wrap round the throat is the shape tell against Greece's open-necked turban and Egypt's full-length izar. The Fuller and Pentney brooches are 9th-century, so the niello disc style is slightly archaic for 1050; later Winchester-style disc brooches are an equally valid reference. The late Anglo-Saxon moment was chosen over Chaucer-era England because the c. 1390 houppelande and hood are too close to Rhineland c. 1440. Uncertain: exact colours, and whether the moustache-only look was universal (older men sometimes wore forked beards).

entries.moment: The Rhine cities of Strasbourg and Mainz, c. 1440, when Johannes Gutenberg was running his first experiments with movable metal type

male.outfit: Calf-length belted gown (Tappert) in deep blue or green wool with regular organ-pipe pleats, a high standing collar and wide, fur-trimmed sleeves, worn over tight hose. Moderately long pointed shoes (Schnabelschuhe).
male.hair: Chin-length straight hair with a full fringe, mostly inside the hood
male.facialHair: none (clean-shaven, the 15th-century norm)
male.headwear: Gugel: a close hood enclosing the head and neck, with the face opening fully clear. It has a short shoulder cape cut into scalloped leaf-shaped points (dags) and ends in a long tail (Zipfel) that hangs down the back.
male.accessory: Low-slung leather belt with a hanging leather purse (Guerteltasche)

female.outfit: Ankle-length, high-waisted wool gown in deep blue or green with long sleeves fitted tight to the wrist, belted just under the bust with a wide girdle, the skirt trailing on the ground. A dark mantle is held at the chest.
female.hair: Hair plaited and pinned up entirely beneath the headdress
female.headwear: Kruseler: a white linen veil edged with several rows of tightly ruffled frills that frame the forehead and cheeks like a halo, with no chin band
female.accessory: Round gold brooch-clasp (Fuerspan / Heftel) at the neckline

entries.signature: Men: the Gugel hood with its scalloped shoulder cape and long tail, plus pointed Schnabelschuhe. Women: the Kruseler veil with its many-layered frilled edge.
avoid: armour, crowns or noble regalia
clerical or monastic robes
the pointed 'Judenhut' or any discriminatory marker or badge
Anglo-Saxon disc-brooch cloak, long moustache or headrail veil (Britain-medieval)
tall conical hennin (Burgundian)
Italian padded ring-hat (mazzocchio) or the women's ghirlanda roll (Italy-medieval)
an ankle-length red citizen's gown (reads as the Florentine lucco)
Crusader tabards or crosses
entries.notes: The entry was sound, with minor fixes. The man's gown moved from 'red or blue' to 'blue or green' so it does not repeat the Florentine red lucco. The shoes are 'moderately' long, because the extreme Schnabelschuh peaked around 1460-80. The woman's 'Kotte' label was dropped: the high-belted gown is the 1430s-40s fashion, while the Kotte is the earlier close-fitting gown. Why this moment: Gutenberg's Strasbourg experiments (c. 1439-44) fall inside the medieval era, which leaves early-modern Germany free for the far more distinctive look of c. 1520. Sources: bloshka.info ('Cruselers'; 'Wulsthaube, Steuchlein') and Wikipedia, '1400-1500 in European fashion'. These show the Kruseler as a Central European frilled veil of the 14th-15th centuries, with the Wulsthaube developing from it only in the second half of the 15th century, so 1440 is late but defensible. Also Hans Multscher's Wurzach Altar (1437), Stefan Lochner (Cologne, 1440s) and the Nuremberg Mendel Housebook (from 1425). Uncertain: dagged Gugel capes peaked in the late 14th century but lasted in German lands well into the 15th.

entries.moment: Ottoman Cairo, c. 1700 (Cairo as hub of the Red Sea coffee trade; the yearly cutting of the Khalij canal dam at the Nile flood)

male.outfit: Ankle-length quftan (kaftan) of saffron or rose silk with small woven stripes or motifs, crossed over the chest. Over it a long, wide-sleeved gibba coat of plain dark broadcloth (forest green or deep blue), open at the front. Wide trousers and pointed red leather slippers.
male.hair: Short-cropped or shaved, hidden under the turban
male.facialHair: Full beard, trimmed short and rounded, with a moustache
male.headwear: Crisp white muslin turban wound in smooth, rounded folds around a red felt cap, with a disc of the red crown left showing on top. The turban cloth is pure white.
male.accessory: Patterned Kashmir or Indian wool shawl wound as a broad sash (hizam) at the waist

female.outfit: Floor-length entari robe of brocaded silk (for example gold on deep rose). Its long sleeves are slit from the elbow to hang open. It is worn over a sheer gauze chemise and wide shintiyan trousers and belted at the hips with a jewelled belt.
female.hair: Long hair in many thin plaits hanging down the back
female.headwear: Tartur: a tall headdress that is wider at the top than at the base, wrapped in black or brown cloth woven with gold stripes. A light gauze veil hangs down the back from it, and the face is fully uncovered.
female.accessory: Long gold earrings with coin drops

entries.signature: A pure-white muslin turban wound around a red cap, with the red crown showing (women: the tall, gold-striped tartur headdress)
avoid: Istanbul court kavuks and giant ceremonial turbans
janissary bork caps or any Ottoman military dress
Mamluk-bey armour and weapons
fez worn alone without a turban (a 19th-century look)
coloured or checked turban cloth, striped camel-hair 'aba cloaks, keffiyeh/agal (read as Iraq)
a small red cap wrapped in a patterned kerchief for the woman (reads as Greece-earlymodern)
face veils that hide the face
odalisque or harem imagery
Mamluk floor-length sleeves (read as Egypt-medieval)
entries.notes: Egypt was an Ottoman province from 1517, so the entry is named 'Ottoman Egypt' and shows local Cairene civilian dress. Sources: Cornelis de Bruyn's travels (published 1698) describe Cairene women in a tall hat wrapped with black or brown cloth woven with gold or silver stripes. Lugatism.com's 'Female attire in Egypt (Ottoman Egypt)' traces the goblet-shaped tartur from Mamluk Cairo through early-17th-century costume books and lists the chemise, shintiyan, zibin, yelek, entari and ferace. The turban wound over a red cap is established by the Mamluk and Ottoman periods and appears in the 1798-1809 Description de l'Egypte costume plates (see also Wikipedia, 'Al-Azhar attire'). Reviewer check: the tartur is now supported by a c. 1700 eyewitness (de Bruyn), not only by older material. If it reads poorly, do NOT fall back to a small red cap with a kerchief, because that would collide with Greece's woman; use a small round cap with a gold-coin fringe instead. Kashmir and Indian shawls reached Cairo through the Red Sea trade. Their use as sashes is best attested later in the 18th century, so treat the pattern as plausible, not certain. Cairo's merchants controlled the Yemen coffee trade, which fits the resources theme.

entries.moment: Baghdad under the governor Hasan Pasha (1704-1723), whose household grew into the Mamluk regime, c. 1720 (notaries recording contracts for the qadi court registers)

male.outfit: Ankle-length zaboun robe of striped cotton-silk (cream with narrow crimson stripes), wrapped across the chest and belted. Over it is an 'aba: a wide, square-shouldered cloak of camel-hair wool with arm slits, woven in broad vertical stripes of dark brown and cream, falling open at the front to mid-calf.
male.hair: Short-cropped, hidden under the turban
male.facialHair: Full beard with a moustache
male.headwear: Loosely wound turban of clearly coloured, patterned cloth (for example cream with fine red-brown checks, or dark indigo with small motifs), with a fringed end tucked in at the side. It is never plain white and never shows a red crown.
male.accessory: Brass qalamdan: a long pen case with an inkwell at one end, tucked upright into the belt

entries.notes: From 1450 to 1750 Baghdad passed between Turkmen, Safavid and Ottoman rule. It was Ottoman from 1638. Hasan Pasha (1704-1723) and his son Ahmad Pasha built the Georgian Mamluk household, and Mamluk pashas ruled in their own right from 1747. The earlier wording 'Mamluk pashas from 1704' was corrected for that reason. The entry shows local Arab townsman dress. Urban dress was broadly shared across the Ottoman Arab provinces, so this design deliberately leans on Iraq-specific elements. One is the striped camel-hair 'aba, an ancient Arab garment still woven in Iraq, for example in Najaf. The other is coloured turban cloths in place of Cairo's white-on-red. The exact turban pattern is the least-attested detail, and no firm local name for it was confirmed. The zaboun, futa and 'asaba are documented in Iraqi traditional dress, but mostly through 19th-century sources, so their use in 1720 is extrapolated. The pen case (Ottoman divit/qalamdan worn in the sash) is well attested for scribes and fits the records theme. Crescents were removed from the necklace as a precaution.

entries.notes: Sources: Recueil Ferriol (1714), after Jean-Baptiste Vanmour's paintings of 1707-08, which includes Greek merchants and Greek women of the Levant. Also Tournefort, 'Relation d'un voyage du Levant' (1717), and the Benaki Museum costume collections. Ottoman dress regulations (see History of Istanbul, 'Clothing and fashion in Istanbul 1453-1923') forbade Christians red kalpaks, yellow shoes and luxury materials such as sable. The design therefore uses a black kalpak, black shoes, fox or lamb fur and silk-cotton alaca instead of pure silk. Contemporary sources describe Greek kalpaks in several shapes, including a sable band round a leather cap and a mitre shape. A plain rounded lambskin shape was chosen to avoid any clergy reading and to set it apart from Ming China's square black gauze cap. Ioannina was a major centre of Greek learning and trade (the Maroutsis and Gioumas schools) with semi-autonomous community councils, which fits the citizenship theme. Uncertain: some Greek merchants, especially islanders, wore dark turbans, and the choice between kalpak and turban varied by town and decade. Ioannina women's dress and the pafti are best documented from the 18th-19th centuries, so they are slightly back-projected.

female.accessory: Long necklace of dark jet beads looped twice around the neck

entries.notes: Sources: the Anonimo Gaddiano records Leonardo wearing a rose-coloured pitocco reaching only to the knee when long gowns were the fashion. The earlier 'pitocco/giornea' was trimmed to 'pitocco', because a giornea is a different, open-sided garment. Leonardo's Portrait of a Musician (c. 1485, Milan) shows the small red berretta and zazzera. His Lady with an Ermine (c. 1489-91) and La Belle Ferronniere show the lenza (with a brow jewel in the latter), the coazzone, the laced sleeves and the dark bead necklace. Beatrice d'Este popularised the coazzone in Milan. The belt notebook is widely repeated in Leonardo lore and fits his own advice to carry a small book, but it is not firmly sourced, so treat it as flavour. The man's shoulder cloak was dropped because it duplicated Britain's man. Galileo (Padua/Florence c. 1610) is the other early-modern figure, but his black Spanish-influenced dress would collide with Britain and Germany, so Leonardo's Milan was kept for distinctiveness. The lenza is thin, so artists should give it the small central jewel so it reads at thumbnail size.

entries.notes: Sources: late-Ming portraits of Jiangnan gentry and women; Wanli-to-Chongzhen genre and woodblock illustrations; excavated Ming garments (for example the Wang Xijue family tomb in Suzhou and the Kong family mansion collection); Tiangong Kaiwu illustrations, whose women wear upright-collared, front-opening jackets over skirts. Reviewer fixes: late-Ming sources show women's ao lengthening to knee length, so the earlier 'hip-length' was corrected. Skirts of the early Chongzhen reign were mostly plain white, so the deep red or green skirt was replaced. The standing collar with metal zimu buttons is a well-attested mid-to-late Ming innovation. The forehead band is attested in Ming women's portraits. Its period names vary (baotou, tougu, and wotu for the fur winter version), so treat the name as moderately uncertain. The man's facial hair was toned down to the neat style seen in Ming portraits, to avoid the drooping-moustache caricature. The jinbu pendant was swapped for gourd earrings, which are well attested in Ming tomb finds, because it duplicated Japan's knee-length tassels. None of the designer's figures falls in this era. The late-Ming printing and knowledge moment fits the theme and keeps this entry clearly apart from the Qing industrial one.

entries.moment: Edo and Sunpu at the founding of the Tokugawa shogunate, c. 1610, in Tokugawa Ieyasu's time. He received a Spanish mechanical clock in 1611.

male.outfit: Kataginu and hakama over a kosode. The kataginu is a sleeveless over-vest with straight, squared shoulders that extend a little past the wearer's own. They lie flat, not yet the stiff, flaring wings of later Edo. The matching pleated hakama are in indigo, grey or brown hemp. Under them is a kosode with small sleeve openings and a fine repeating pattern, collar crossing left over right. No crests.
male.hair: Chasen-mage: shaved pate (sakayaki), with the remaining hair gathered at the crown into a short upright topknot bound with white cord like a tea whisk
male.facialHair: Thin moustache and a small chin beard
male.headwear: none
male.accessory: Inro: a small stacked lacquered case hanging from the sash on a silk cord, held by a carved netsuke toggle

female.headwear: none

entries.notes: Sources: Keicho- and Kan'ei-era kosode (Tokyo National Museum); Momoyama to early Edo genre screens (Rakuchu-rakugai-zu, the Hikone screen); inro, which appear from the late 16th century. Reviewer fix: Japanese costume histories (Japanese Wiki Corpus, 'Kamishimo') say kataginu shoulders were widened during the Edo period and reached about a foot around the Genroku era (1688-1703), when whale baleen was first inserted to make them stand out. The earlier 'stiff winged shoulders' was therefore about 80 years too late for 1610. The vest is now drawn with modest squared shoulders, and the thumbnail tell rests on the sleeveless vest, the hakama, and the bare shaved-pate topknot (the only hatless man in this era). The kataginu and hakama were the civil formal dress of officials, and townsmen of standing also wore them. This is not military dress. Crests were removed entirely to avoid any real clan or regime emblem. Ieyasu's Spanish clock (Kunozan Toshogu) ties this moment to the precision and automation theme. The Nagoya-obi cord belt belongs to the late 16th and early 17th centuries and disappears by mid-century, which keeps this entry distinct from later Edo. Uncertain: inro were only just coming into use c. 1610; a kinchaku drawstring pouch on a cord is a safe fallback.

entries.moment: The Royal Exchange in London, c. 1600, the year the East India Company received its charter

male.facialHair: Pointed 'pick-a-devant' beard with an upturned moustache
male.headwear: Tall-crowned black felt capotain hat with a narrow brim and a plain hatband
male.accessory: A single pearl-drop earring in one ear

female.headwear: Tall-crowned black felt hat with a narrow brim, worn over the white coif (the London citizen's wife's hat)

entries.notes: Sources: portraits of London merchants and citizens from the 1590s to the 1610s. Hollar's Ornatus Muliebris Anglicanus (1640) shows the tradition of London citizen wives in tall hats over coifs, and tall-crowned hats on women already appear in portraits of the 1590s-1600s. Janet Arnold, 'Patterns of Fashion' and 'Queen Elizabeth's Wardrobe Unlock'd', cover the doublet, Venetians and ruff construction. Men's pearl earrings are well documented in portraits (for example Drake and Raleigh). They are more courtly than mercantile, but plausible for a prosperous Exchange merchant. Why this moment: the East India Company (1600) and the Royal Exchange (1571) fit Britain's trade-network theme, and none of the designer's British figures falls in this era. Reviewer check: no changes needed for accuracy. The ruff is safe here because Germany is set at c. 1525, before ruffs existed. The tall brimmed hat is distinct from Greece's brimless fur kalpak and China's square gauze cap, because only Britain pairs it with a ruff and visible breeches and stockings.

entries.moment: Nuremberg c. 1525: Duerer's city and Europe's hub of printing and precision instruments (Henlein's early portable spring-driven clocks, Behaim's globe), the year the city council adopted the Reformation as Luther's printed pamphlets spread

male.facialHair: Full, rounded beard with a moustache, trimmed fairly short (the new German fashion of the 1520s)
male.headwear: Wide, flat black velvet Barett with a slashed brim, worn tilted to one side
male.accessory: Heavy gold link chain draped across the shoulders and chest

female.outfit: Red or black wool gown with a laced bodice, a full pleated skirt and sleeves banded with horizontal puffs and slashes. It is worn over a high-necked pleated white linen shirt with a gold-embroidered collar band, and a short black velvet shoulder cape (Goller) covers the shoulders.

female.headwear: Wide, flat Barett tilted to one side over the hairnet, trimmed with a small white feather
female.accessory: Several layered gold chains across the chest

entries.notes: Sources: Duerer's 1526 Nuremberg portraits of Hieronymus Holzschuher (full beard), Jakob Muffel and Johann Kleberger, and his portrait of Jakob Fugger (c. 1518). Also Lucas Cranach the Elder's portraits of Saxon burghers and their wives, and Hans Holbein the Younger's Georg Gisze (1532, a Hanseatic merchant). The Kolbe haircut, Kuhmaulschuhe, Schaube and Goller are standard German costume-history terms for c. 1500-1540. Reviewer fix: the original man (clean-shaven, chin-length bob with a fringe, cap, knee-length coat) was nearly the same figure as Italy's Leonardo-era man at thumbnail size. The moment was moved to c. 1525, when beards came back into German fashion (Holzschuher 1526; Luther's 1521-22 beard). The man now has a full beard and the shorter 1520s hair, which, with the wide tilted Barett and fur collar, separates him clearly from Italy. 'Early pocket watches' was softened to 'portable spring-driven clocks', because the pocket-watch attribution to Henlein is disputed. Uncertain: married Nuremberg burgher women often wore a white linen Wulsthaube or the large church headdress (Stuerz) instead of a Barett. The Barett over a gold hairnet is better attested for younger women and wealthier burghers, as in Cranach. It was chosen because it reads at thumbnail size and matches the men's signature. A white roll headdress could also be mistaken for a turban next to the Ottoman-era entries.

male.hair: Short and neatly trimmed, mostly hidden under the tarboush
male.facialHair: Full, neatly groomed moustache with a clean-shaven chin
male.headwear: Tarboush: a stiff, upright, flat-topped cap of deep-crimson felt, shaped like a truncated cone and set straight and level on the head. A short black silk tassel falls from the centre of the crown toward the back. It is never floppy or tilted.
male.accessory: Gold watch-chain hanging from a coat button to the breast pocket

female.outfit: Yelek: an ankle-length, fitted, long-sleeved robe of striped silk (cream with rose and gold stripes), buttoned from bust to hips and slit open at the sides below. It is worn over a sheer chemise and full shintiyan trousers gathered at the ankle, and girdled at the hips with a folded Kashmir shawl.

female.headwear: Tarha: a long white muslin head veil with its ends embroidered in coloured silk and gold thread. entries.notes: FIXED DATE: the Ottoman firman granting Isma'il the title of Khedive is dated 8 June 1867 (Wikipedia, 'Isma'il Pasha of Egypt' and 'Khedive'), so a 'Khedivate' in 1865 was anachronistic. The date is moved to 1869, when the canal opened. Sources: E.W. Lane, 'Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians' (1836). Lane describes the tarha as a long white muslin veil embroidered at each end in coloured silks and gold, resting on the head and hanging down behind nearly to the ground, worn over a tarboosh wound with a faroodiyeh kerchief. The kirdan is documented as an Ottoman-type choker worn in gold by urban Cairene women in the 19th century, with crescent pendants ('kirdan hilali'); see bedouinsilver.com and see.news. The effendiya wore the tarboush and stambouline from the 1820s to the 1950s. CHANGED: the women's red tarboush with gold kurs is no longer the visible headwear. It is documented c. 1835 and uncertain for 1869, and a small red cap would clash with the Greek women's fesi. The white tarha is kept as the women's tell. COMPROMISE: this is Cairene indoor or visiting dress. Outdoors she would have worn the habara and burqu', which hide the face and are not allowed in this game. The traveller is a civilian canal or irrigation engineer, which fits the infrastructure theme.

entries.notes: Sources: Wikipedia, 'Al-Zaura', and the Library of Congress holdings (Midhat Pasha brought a printing press from Paris; al-Zawra was the first Iraqi newspaper, from 1869), which fits the records and knowledge theme. The agal is a doubled black animal-hair cord that holds the keffiyeh (FIT Fashion History Timeline, 'agal'). UNCERTAINTY: Baghdad men c. 1870 wore a mix of turbans (notables and clergy), the fez (effendis and officials) and the headcloth with 'igal (Arab merchants and tribal visitors). The Wikipedia 'Sidara' article does not document pre-1920s Baghdad headwear, and a general source says Levantine townsmen favoured the fez. The headcloth is therefore a plausible, not dominant, townsman look, chosen for distinctiveness because Egypt owns the fez. CHANGED: the headcloth is now plain white, to avoid chequered patterns with modern political associations. The 'aba is now camel-brown, so it cannot be read as Italy's black tabarro and differs from the woman's black 'abaya. The signet ring was replaced by a brass pen-case (dawat). A ring is invisible at thumbnail size, while the pen-case tucked in the girdle was a standard worn item of Ottoman-world scribes and merchants and suits the records theme.

entries.moment: Athens, new capital of the independent Greek kingdom, c. 1860

male.outfit: Civilian fustanella: a white, many-pleated linen kilt ending just above the knee, a full-sleeved white shirt, and a dark-crimson sleeveless jacket (fermeli) trimmed with gold braid and worn open over an embroidered waistcoat. Below are knitted white stockings with tasselled garters and plain black leather shoes.
male.hair: Short on top, slightly longer at the nape
male.facialHair: Thick moustache with slightly upturned ends
male.headwear: Fesi: a soft Greek fez of red felt whose limp crown droops to one side, worn tilted, with a very long dark-blue silk tassel falling to the chest. It is clearly floppy, unlike Egypt's stiff, upright tarboush.
male.accessory: Wide red silk sash (zonari) wound around the waist

female.outfit: Amalia dress: a floor-length full skirt of pale ivory or rose silk, a white long-sleeved blouse with a lace chemisette front, and a short, fitted, open bolero jacket (kontogouni) of deep-burgundy velvet heavily embroidered with gold braid.
female.hair: Long hair plaited into two braids and wound around the base of the fesi
female.headwear: Small red fesi pinned tilted on the crown, with a long tassel of braided gold thread falling to the shoulder. The face and hairline are fully visible.
female.accessory: Necklace of small gold coins on a chain (dowry flouria)

entries.signature: Men: the white, many-pleated fustanella kilt. Women: the gold-embroidered velvet kontogouni bolero with a small tilted red fesi and a gold tassel.

entries.notes: Sources: Benaki Museum and Peloponnesian Folklore Foundation collections, and mid-19th-century Athenian photographs. Greek City Times, 'Greek traditional Amalia costume', and the academia.edu article 'Amalia Dress: The Invention of a New Costume Tradition' (Catwalk, 2012) describe the costume: a red fesi with a long tassel of braided gold thread worn at an angle, and a short, close-fitting, gold-embroidered velvet kontogouni. The Amalia dress was promoted by Queen Amalia (1837-1862) but widely adopted as urban bourgeois 'national' dress, so depict it as middle-class civilian wear. CHANGED: the jacket colours are now dark crimson (men) and burgundy (women), and the skirt ivory or rose. Blue velvet over a pale skirt is historical but would read as a flag-colour scheme. The fesi descriptions were sharpened, soft and drooping with a long tassel for men and a gold tassel for women, because Egypt's men wear a red tarboush. The women's signature now leads with the kontogouni, so a red cap is not the only tell. Athenian men of 1860 were split between the fustanella and western frock coats, and the fustanella was chosen as the clear Greek tell. Keep it civilian: no weapons and no pom-pom shoes.

entries.moment: Bologna and Pontecchio, where young Guglielmo Marconi ran his first radio experiments, 1895

male.outfit: Dark wool three-piece suit with a white shirt, stiff standing collar and dark cravat. Over it is a full, calf-length circular tabarro cloak in black or midnight-blue wool, with a velvet collar and a metal chain clasp at the throat. One side is flung back over the opposite shoulder, showing the suit.
male.hair: Short, side-parted and pomaded
male.facialHair: Full, thick moustache brushed outward in the 'Umbertine' fashion, not waxed to points
male.headwear: Wide-brimmed soft black felt hat with a low rounded crown and a broad, slightly drooping brim (the hat worn with the tabarro in the Po Valley)
male.accessory: Long white silk scarf hanging loose around the neck under the open cloak, in the style of Verdi

female.outfit: Mid-1890s dress in dark wool: a fitted bodice with a high collar, puffed leg-of-mutton sleeves and a smooth, bell-shaped, floor-length skirt. A large black silk scialle (shawl) with a long knotted fringe is draped over the shoulders and crossed at the chest.
female.hair: Swept up into a high chignon with a soft curled fringe
female.headwear: none
female.accessory: Multi-strand red coral bead necklace worn over the high collar

entries.signature: Men: the tabarro, a full dark circular cloak with a velvet collar and one side flung over the opposite shoulder, worn with a broad-brimmed black felt hat. Women: the black fringed silk scialle crossed over the chest, with a red coral necklace.
