entries.notes: Sources: the tabarro is documented as the cloak of Emilia-Romagna and Veneto landowners and townsmen. Verdi wore it, and Italians were so identified with it that emigrants to America were recognised by it (tabarro.it history, costume references). Coral jewellery (the Torre del Greco industry) was a ubiquitous Italian adornment. The fringed black scialle is best documented for Venetian and north-Italian townswomen c. 1880-1910. Leg-of-mutton sleeves peaked around 1893-97, which fits 1895. CHANGED: the lobbia (a soft felt hat with a lengthwise crown dent and medium brim) was replaced by a broad-brimmed soft felt. At thumbnail size the lobbia is nearly identical to Germany's Homburg, and broad-brimmed felts are the usual companion of the tabarro in Po-Valley imagery; this pairing is a moderate-confidence visual, and a web search did not return a firm source. The moustache is now bushy rather than curled, so it is not mistaken for Germany's waxed style. UNCERTAIN: by 1895 the tabarro was increasingly a provincial or older man's garment; a fashionable 21-year-old like Marconi more often wore an overcoat and bowler. Marconi also falls in the modern era, but 1895 was used here so modern Italy can take a more distinctive 1960 look.

entries.moment: Shanghai in the late Qing, c. 1880: the Shenbao newspaper, the Jiangnan Arsenal translation bureau and the first telegraph lines

male.outfit: Changshan: an ankle-length gown in dark-blue or grey silk with a small standing collar and a curved diagonal (dajin) opening fastened by cloth knot buttons down the right side. Over it is a magua: a short, hip-length black jacket with a straight centre opening, knot buttons and roomy sleeves. Black cloth shoes with white soles.
male.hair: Queue: the front of the scalp shaved back to the crown and the rest braided into one long, neat plait down the back. Draw it tidily and with dignity, never as a caricature.
male.facialHair: none (clean-shaven; by Qing custom moustaches were usually grown only in middle age)
male.headwear: Guapimao: a rounded black satin skullcap of six segments with a red knotted-silk button on top and no official finial
male.accessory: Hebao: a small embroidered silk purse on a knotted silk cord with a tassel, hanging from the waist belt at the right hip just below the hem of the magua

female.outfit: Ao: a loose, knee-length jacket with wide flared sleeves and a curved right-side opening with knot buttons. Its collar edge, front curve, cuffs and hem are covered in several broad bands of contrasting embroidered trim (xianggun). The jacket is lotus-pink or pale blue with black trim, worn over a black pleated mamian skirt.
female.hair: Sleek and centre-parted, combed smoothly back into a flat low bun at the nape and pinned with a silver hairpin
female.headwear: Meile (brow band): a narrow band of black satin worn across the forehead just above the brows and tied at the back. It is embroidered with small flowers and set with a small pearl or jade ornament at centre front, and leaves the face fully visible.
female.accessory: Green jade bangle bracelet

entries.signature: Men: the black six-segment guapimao skullcap with a red knot button, worn with the queue. Women: the broad-trimmed ao jacket with a black embroidered meile band across the forehead.
avoid: 19th-century Western 'pigtail' cartoons, Fu Manchu or long drooping moustache, slanted-eye features

entries.notes: Sources: John Thomson's photographs of China (1868-72); Shanghai studio portraits of the 1870s-80s; Dianshizhai Pictorial (1884-98). For the meile: Baidu Baike, 'Forehead Band'; newhanfu.com, 'The Headwear Mo'e'; and the Metropolitan Museum's woman's headdress of the Guangxu period (1875-1908). Forehead bands of silk or satin, embroidered and set with pearls or jade, were worn by Qing women of every rank. The queue was a legally imposed Qing hairstyle for Han men and must be drawn respectfully. The broad multi-band trim on Han women's jackets peaked in the late 19th century. CHANGED: the long, thin moustache drooping past the mouth was removed; it is effectively the 'Fu Manchu' look the avoid list bans. The round spectacles were replaced by a hebao purse so the look does not overlap with Germany's pince-nez. A meile headband was added so the woman has a thumbnail-distinct headwear tell. The short fringe was removed from her hair: bangs became fashionable mainly in the 1890s-1900s and would sit under the band. UNCERTAIN: the meile was worn especially in cooler months. None of the designer's figures falls in this era.

entries.moment: Nagoya in the Meiji period, c. 1899, the time of Sakichi Toyoda's steam-powered wooden loom (1896) and Japan's rapid industrialisation

male.outfit: Dark kimono under a knee-length black haori with small white generic family crests (never the chrysanthemum), over grey-and-black striped pleated hakama. White tabi socks and zori sandals. The kimono collar crosses left over right.
male.hair: Zangiri: a short, Western-style, side-parted crop (topknots were abandoned after 1871)
male.facialHair: Neat, trimmed moustache, straight and not waxed to points
male.headwear: Black Western bowler hat (yamataka-bo) with a rigid round dome and a narrow brim
male.accessory: Haori-himo: a thick white braided silk cord tied in a flat knot with two tassels at the centre of the chest, closing the haori

female.outfit: Jogakusei (girl student) look: a small-patterned kimono, e.g. with purple-and-white yagasuri arrow-feather stripes, under a maroon (ebicha) pleated hakama tied high above the waist. Tabi with zori or low boots. The kimono collar crosses left over right.
female.hair: Sokuhatsu: hair swept up and back into a puffed pompadour roll with a bun at the back of the head (Western-inspired, promoted from 1885)
female.headwear: none
female.accessory: Large silk ribbon bow tied at the back of the sokuhatsu

entries.signature: Men: a black bowler hat worn with a crested haori, white himo cord and striped hakama, a Western hat over Japanese dress. Women: the maroon hakama tied high over a yagasuri kimono, with sokuhatsu hair and a ribbon bow.
avoid: Imperial Army or Navy uniforms, the Rising Sun flag, the sixteen-petal imperial chrysanthemum

entries.notes: Sources: Meiji photography (Felice Beato, Kusakabe Kimbei); Chikanobu's prints of sokuhatsu styles (1880s); the 1871 Danpatsurei; Toyota Industries' history of the 1896 Toyoda power loom. Wikipedia's 'Utako Shimoda' and 'Jissen Women's University' articles confirm her hakama reform and the founding of her girls' school in 1899. CHANGED: the pocket-watch chain was replaced with the haori-himo cord, because Egypt and Britain also wear watch chains; the himo is a distinctly Japanese worn item and reads at thumbnail size. The moustache is now straight, to separate it from Germany's waxed upturned style. The footwear is now a single choice. UNCERTAIN: women students' hakama spread c. 1899-1905, and hair ribbons became a schoolgirl fad mainly c. 1900-05, so both are at the early edge for 1899. Portraits of Sakichi Toyoda show a moustache, but this is unconfirmed by a source. Hokusai (c. 1831) also falls in this era, but a late-Edo look would be hard to tell apart from the earlymodern entry. Toyoda's automatic loom (Type G, 1924) belongs to the modern era if the team prefers him there.

entries.moment: London in 1843, when Ada Lovelace published her notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine, as the Cooke-Wheatstone electric telegraph spread and just before Railway Mania (1845-47)

male.outfit: Knee-length black or bottle-green wool frock coat with a nipped waist and full skirt, over a patterned silk waistcoat and narrow fawn or checked trousers. A white shirt with tall collar points, wrapped with a wide black silk neck-stock or cravat.
male.hair: Side-parted hair, full and curled over the ears
male.facialHair: Mutton-chop side-whiskers running down the jaw, with the upper lip and chin clean-shaven
male.headwear: Tall black silk top hat (stovepipe) with a slightly curled brim
male.accessory: Gold pocket-watch chain looped across the waistcoat

female.outfit: Day dress with a tight bodice that comes to a point at the waist, low sloping shoulders, narrow long sleeves and a full bell-shaped skirt over layered petticoats. It is made in dark plaid silk or printed cotton, with a small white lace collar.
female.hair: Early-Victorian centre parting: hair smoothed flat over the crown, with clusters of ringlets over each ear and a bun at the back
female.headwear: Deep straw poke ('coal-scuttle') bonnet that frames the face, tied under the chin with a wide ribbon. The face stays fully visible.
female.accessory: Large Paisley shawl, woven in Paisley, Scotland, with the teardrop 'boteh' pattern, draped around the shoulders

entries.signature: Men: a tall black silk top hat with mutton-chop whiskers and a clean upper lip. Women: a coal-scuttle bonnet with a Paisley shawl.
avoid: redcoat, police, guards or any uniform
Union Jack or royal regalia

entries.notes: Sources: fashion plates and daguerreotypes from 1840-1845, V&A collection day dresses, and C. Willett Cunnington on English women's dress of the 19th century. Paisley shawl production peaked in the 1840s-60s. CHANGED: the moment text said 1843 was 'the height of Railway Mania', but the mania peaked in 1845-47, so it now says 'just before'. In early-Victorian Britain men wore side-whiskers, but civilian moustaches were uncommon (they were associated with the military and with foreigners). That makes the clean upper lip a useful contrast with the German moustache. Lovelace's year was chosen over Watt's Birmingham (c. 1780) because it covers steam, railways, telegraphs and computing together. UNCERTAIN: the name 'Albert chain' for the watch chain probably dates from later in the 1840s, so it is not used. The watch chain overlaps with Egypt's accessory, which is acceptable because the top hat and bonnet are the tells.

entries.moment: Berlin c. 1899, during the boom in German electrical engineering (Siemens, AEG) and chemistry (Bayer's aspirin, synthetic dyes), when Berlin's permanent dress-reform exhibition opened

male.outfit: Dark charcoal wool frock coat (Gehrock) buttoned high over a matching waistcoat, with narrow dark striped trousers. A very tall, stiff white stand-up collar (Stehkragen) with a narrow dark tie.
male.hair: Short brush cut (Buerstenschnitt): hair cropped close and standing upright
male.facialHair: Moustache with the ends twisted up in the Wilhelmine 'Es ist erreicht' fashion, kept moderate rather than pointed up to the cheekbones
male.headwear: Dark felt Homburg with a single dent down the centre of the crown and a stiff, curled-up, ribbon-bound brim (named after Bad Homburg in Hesse)
male.accessory: Pince-nez (Kneifer) clipped to the nose, on a thin black cord

female.outfit: Reformkleid: a loose, uncorseted, floor-length dress hanging straight from a fitted shoulder yoke, with soft full sleeves, in sage-green, cream or dove-grey wool. The yoke and hem are embroidered with flowing Jugendstil plant curves.
female.hair: Soft, loose chignon: hair pinned up low and full at the back, with natural waves at the temples
female.headwear: none
female.accessory: Jugendstil silver-and-enamel brooch at the collar in the Pforzheim style, with a curving 'whiplash' leaf motif

entries.signature: Men: a Homburg hat with pince-nez and an upturned moustache. Women: a loose, uncorseted Reformkleid with Jugendstil embroidery on the yoke.

Iron Cross, eagle emblems, black-white-red imperial colours

entries.notes: Sources: Berliner Zeitung, 'Um des Kaisers Bart', and de.wikipedia 'Schnurrbart'. Court barber Francois Haby's 'Es ist erreicht' moustache band was used across social classes in the Wilhelmine era. Wikipedia, 'Deutscher Verband Frau und Kultur', and LEO-BW on Reformkleidung: the Verein fuer Verbesserung der Frauenkleidung was founded in Berlin in 1896, held its first exhibition in April 1897, and had a permanent exhibition from 1899. The Homburg takes its name from Bad Homburg and was popularised abroad by Edward VII. Theodor Fahrner of Pforzheim made Jugendstil jewellery (c. 1900, so right at the edge of 1899). CHANGED: the moustache was toned down to a moderate twist. The brush cut, pince-nez and extreme Kaiser points together would tip into the 'stern Prussian' caricature; the moustache is a civilian fashion, not insignia. UNCERTAIN: in 1899 the Reformkleid was a progressive minority choice, and a typical Berlin woman wore a corseted skirt suit with leg-of-mutton sleeves. That would collide with Italy's 1895 dress, so the Reformkleid is kept as the distinctly German option. None of the designer's German figures falls in this era; Haber's ammonia work comes in 1909.

entries.moment: Egypt under Gamal Abdel Nasser, Cairo and Aswan, c. 1962 (Aswan High Dam under construction 1960-70; Suez Canal nationalised 1956)

male.outfit: Ankle-length galabiya of fine pale-grey or finely striped cotton (loose and collarless, with a deep slit neckline and wide sleeves), worn with a tailored dark Western suit jacket open over it; leather shoes.
male.hair: Short hair combed straight back from a high forehead
male.facialHair: Thick, neat moustache, otherwise clean-shaven
male.headwear: none (bareheaded; the tarboush was abandoned after the 1952 revolution)
male.accessory: Shal: a long, plain dark wool scarf (brown, charcoal or camel) with a knotted fringe, draped round the neck so both ends hang straight down the chest outside the jacket. No stripes.

female.outfit: Village or provincial galabiya: an ankle-length, loose, long-sleeved dress in brightly printed cotton (small flowers on a saturated red, green or blue ground), with a round neck and a gathered yoke, often finished with a gathered flounce at the hem. Flat slippers.
female.hair: Long hair, centre-parted, in one thick plait hanging down the back below the scarf. Only the parting and a little front hair show.
female.headwear: Mandil abu oya: a coloured triangular cotton or chiffon headscarf tied at the back of the head (knot at the nape, point covering the back of the head), its front edge trimmed with a fringe of tiny crocheted flowers or beads that frames the forehead. Face, chin and neck fully visible.
female.accessory: Ghawayesh: a stack of thick gold bangles on each wrist

entries.signature: The galabiya. Men wear a tailored Western jacket over it. Women wear a bright printed galabiya with a flower-edged mandil tied at the nape.
avoid: tarboush or fez (reads as Egypt-industrial)

entries.notes: The country's official name from 1958 to 1971 was the United Arab Republic, so the entry uses 'Nasser's Egypt'. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Egyptian cultural dress'; the Wikipedia 'Sidara' article (the fez survived among Egypt's effendiya only into the early 1950s). A suit jacket over a galabiya was widely worn by provincial merchants and village notables in mid-century Egypt and reads as Egypt instantly. The female look was REPLACED. The earlier 1960s Cairo look (bouffant, sheath dress, big dark sunglasses) matched Rome 1960 almost item for item. The new look pairs with the provincial man. The mandil abu oya is a triangular kerchief that was a core part of the fellaha dress, worn with the galabiya fellahi in the Delta, Upper Egypt and on the coasts; today it survives mostly in poorer quarters and as fancy dress (Youm7, 17 Apr 2025; al-Ain; elfagr.org). Gold bangles were the traditional form of a village woman's savings. Draw the mandil respectfully: the knot sits at the back, not under the chin, and the face stays uncovered. If an urban Cairo woman is required, she needs a new Egypt-only tell. Do not reuse sunglasses or a bouffant.

entries.moment: Baghdad c. 1956, the Development Board's modernist building boom (commissions for Gropius, Le Corbusier and Wright) in the city where Zaha Hadid grew up

male.outfit: Light-grey or tan wool two-piece suit with wide lapels, white shirt, dark tie and polished shoes.

male.facialHair: Neatly trimmed moustache
male.headwear: Sidara (al-Faisaliyya): a soft black felt or velvet civilian cap that folds flat; it is boat-shaped, with a raised point at front and back and a lengthwise crease along the crown, worn straight on the head with no badge

female.headwear: The top edge of the black 'abaya resting on the crown of the head, leaving the face and front hair visible
female.accessory: Gold coin pendant: a single large gold coin (lira) on a short gold chain, visible at the neckline where the 'abaya falls open

entries.notes: Sources: Wikipedia, 'Sidara'. King Faisal I introduced it after 1921 as national headwear, deliberately distinct from the Ottoman fez and the Arabian ghutra-and-agal. Its popularity declined gradually after the monarchy fell in 1958, and it is now worn mainly at ceremonies and weddings. The moment is set just before 1958 so the sidara is still current. Draw it clearly as a civilian cap: soft black and badge-free. Also IRFAD, 'Iraq Fashion' (1950s Baghdad dress was strongly Western and progressive). Zaha Hadid was born in Baghdad in 1950. Many educated Baghdad women stopped wearing the 'abaya in the 1950s and 60s, but it was still common and is used here as the female tell. It also appears on Iraq-industrial; there the dress underneath differs. CHANGED: the pearl strand became a gold coin pendant, because pearls are Britain's modern tell (twinset and pearls) and a leaked strand would not read as foreign. Uncertain: gold lira pendants are a well-attested regional gift of gold, but I could not find a specific 1950s Baghdad source. If the team objects, a wide gold bracelet is the fallback. Egypt's stacked bangles differ enough to allow it.

entries.notes: Sources: the tagari was the Greek shepherd's woven wool bag (PieceWork, 'From Sheep to Tagari'). In the 1970s it became so emblematic of Athenian students in jeans, boots and wide wool sweaters that 'tagari' was period slang for them (slang.gr). That slang was derogatory, so do not use it as a label in-game. The Polytechnic uprising (Nov 1973) and the Metapolitefsi fit the citizenship and public-debate theme. CHANGED: the man's black fisherman's cap was dropped. At thumbnail size its soft crown and short peak read the same as Beijing 1972's navy cap, and the cap is not Greece-specific anyway (the Breton cap, the Hamburg Elbsegler and the 'Lennon cap' are near-identical). A bareheaded student also fits 1975 better. The tagari now carries Greece for both sexes; keep its stripes bold and its fringe visible so it cannot be mistaken for China's plain satchel. Flat handmade leather sandals were an Athenian craft staple.

entries.moment: Rome during the economic miracle, the year of 'La Dolce Vita', 1960

male.outfit: Slim, sharply tailored single-breasted suit in charcoal or midnight mohair-wool, with a short jacket, narrow lapels and narrow cropped trousers. Worn with a crisp white shirt and thin dark tie (or a fine-knit black turtleneck, the 'dolcevita') and polished slip-on loafers.
male.hair: Short, neatly slicked back with pomade
male.facialHair: none
male.headwear: none
male.accessory: Dark sunglasses with solid black lenses and heavy black frames

female.outfit: Fitted knee-length sleeveless sheath dress with a narrow waist in a bold, swirling kaleidoscopic silk print (magenta, turquoise, lime) in the 1960s Florentine style, with pointed low-heeled pumps.
female.hair: Short, voluminous backcombed bouffant, left uncovered
female.headwear: none
female.accessory: Cat-eye sunglasses with dark lenses

entries.signature: Dark sunglasses: men wear them with a razor-slim tailored suit; women wear cat-eye sunglasses with a swirling kaleidoscopic silk-print sheath and an uncovered bouffant
avoid: Fascist-era black shirt, fasces or any 1920s-40s regime insignia
military or carabinieri uniforms
mafia or gangster caricature (pinstripes, fedora, violin case)
pizza-chef, gondolier striped shirt and straw boater stereotypes
Vespa or other held or ridden props
priest's collar or clerical dress (sacred)
headscarf knotted under the chin (now Britain modern's tell)
woven crossbody bag or fisherman's cap (reads 1970s Greece)
orange-padded headphones or lapel badge (reads Japan 1980)
entries.notes: Sources: Fellini's 'La Dolce Vita' (1960) and Roman street photography of the paparazzi era. Italian tailoring (Brioni, Roman and Neapolitan cut) defined the 'Continental' slim suit. Emilio Pucci's kaleidoscopic Florentine prints were the signature Italian women's print of the 1960s; describe the style without naming the brand. In Italian the turtleneck is called a 'dolcevita' after the film. CHANGED: the woman's headscarf was removed. It duplicated Britain 1950's under-chin headscarf, and it would have flattened and hidden the bouffant, which is the point of the Dolce Vita look. Rome's women now read through the print plus the cat-eye sunglasses. Because Egypt's former look (bouffant, sheath, big sunglasses) has been replaced, sunglasses are now Italy-only in this era. Risk: the man's slim dark suit is close to Japan 1980's salaryman suit, so the black sunglasses must always be drawn. Marconi (d. 1937) also falls in the modern era, but his 1920s-30s moment overlaps the Fascist period and is visually generic, so it was used for the industrial entry instead.

entries.moment: Beijing, c. 1972, when Tu Youyou's Project 523 team isolated artemisinin at the Academy of Traditional Chinese Medicine

male.outfit: Zhongshan suit: loose, boxy grey or navy-blue cotton-wool jacket with a closed turn-down collar, five front buttons and four patch pockets with buttoned flaps, worn with matching straight, roomy trousers and black cloth slip-on shoes.
male.hair: Short, neat side-parted crop
male.facialHair: none
male.headwear: Soft navy cotton cap with a tall, rounded, slightly stiffened crown, a cloth band and a short stiff peak. It sits high on the head, unlike a low flat cap. Plain, with no badge or star.
male.accessory: Fountain pen clipped in the upper-left chest pocket, the 1970s mark of an educated professional

female.outfit: Women's version of the same jacket in pale blue or grey cotton, with turn-down collar and patch pockets and a white shirt collar folded out over it. Straight dark trousers and black cloth strap shoes; practical and unornamented.
female.hair: Short, straight, chin-length bob with a side part, held back on one side by a plain black hair clip
female.headwear: none
female.accessory: Plain faded-khaki canvas satchel on a cross-body strap, with no star, slogan, print or stripes

entries.signature: Blue-grey Zhongshan (Mao) suit with four patch pockets, worn by men and women alike
avoid: Mao badges or portrait pins
Red-star cap badge, green PLA uniform, Red Guard armbands
Little Red Book, slogans, any propaganda text
1930s qipao or Shanghai glamour (wrong decade)
White lab coat as the main garment (not culturally distinctive)
Coolie hat or any caricature
Japanese salaryman suit and tie
low flat tweed cap (Britain modern)
striped or fringed woven bag (Greece modern)
entries.notes: Sources: 1970s documentary photographs of Beijing street and workplace dress; photos of Tu Youyou in the Project 523 period (short hair, plain cotton jacket). The Zhongshan suit predates the PRC (Sun Yat-sen, 1920s) and is a garment, not an insignia. Keep it completely free of badges, stars and slogans to meet the no-regime-insignia rule. CLARIFIED: the cap's tall rounded crown and high position are now spelled out so it is not drawn like Britain 1950's low tweed flat cap; Greece's former fisherman's cap was dropped for the same reason. The satchel was the ubiquitous plain canvas bag of the time; keep it plain and unstriped so it cannot be mistaken for Greece's tagari. If the team wants a less politically loaded modern China, the alternative is 1930s Shanghai (qipao, changshan and fedora), but that moves away from Tu Youyou's moment.

entries.moment: Tokyo during the Walkman boom, c. 1980, as Akio Morita's Sony took Japanese electronics global

male.outfit: Salaryman suit: dark navy or charcoal single-breasted two-piece with a white shirt and a narrow dark tie, plus a small round enamel company badge (shasho) with a generic abstract mark on the left lapel; black leather shoes.
male.hair: Short hair neatly combed back with a side part
male.facialHair: none
male.headwear: none
male.accessory: Lightweight silver-and-black headband headphones with round bright-orange foam ear pads worn on the head, a thin cord running to a compact blue-and-silver cassette player in a small tan leather case hooked on the belt; no brand logo

female.outfit: Office lady (OL) company uniform: a fitted navy or burgundy waistcoat over a white blouse with a soft ribbon bow at the collar, a matching knee-length pleated skirt, sheer stockings and low pumps.
female.hair: Seiko-chan cut: layered, shoulder-length feathered bob with soft inward flicks at the sides and wispy bangs (the c. 1980 pop-idol trend)
female.headwear: none
female.accessory: The same orange-foam headphones resting around the neck

entries.signature: Orange-foam headphones worn with a portable cassette player
avoid: Rising Sun flag or rays, or a hachimaki headband with the hinomaru
WWII military uniforms or imagery
Sony or any real brand logo
Anime or manga caricature, samurai or geisha cliches
Kimono (not everyday wear at this moment)
Chinese Zhongshan suit
dark sunglasses (reads as 1960 Rome, whose slim suit is close to the salaryman's)
entries.notes: Sources: the Sony Walkman TPS-L2 (blue-and-silver metal case, on sale in Japan from 1 July 1979, sold with a leather carry case) and its MDR-3L2 headphones with circular orange foam pads (Cooper Hewitt collection; Walkman Archive). Also 1970s-80s Japanese office uniform photography and the Seiko Matsuda hairstyle craze of 1980. Morita is the designer's figure. The salaryman suit alone is generic worldwide and close to Italy 1960's slim suit, so always draw the orange headphones and the lapel badge. The Walkman spread abroad later in the 1980s, so at c. 1980 the headphones still read as distinctly Japanese. Minor edit: the cassette player now sits in its leather case on the belt rather than being 'clipped' on. The original model shipped with a case, not a belt clip.

entries.moment: Manchester, c. 1950, where Alan Turing was working on the university's pioneering stored-program computer (the Manchester Mark 1, built commercially by Ferranti)

male.outfit: Brown herringbone tweed sports jacket with leather elbow patches over a Fair Isle-patterned sleeveless knitted pullover, a white shirt and a knitted wool tie. Baggy grey flannel trousers and brown brogues.
male.hair: Short back and sides: neatly cut, side-parted and slicked with hair cream
male.facialHair: none
male.headwear: Tweed flat cap: low, flat crown sloping forward onto a short peak
male.accessory: Long college scarf in broad block stripes of two contrasting colours, wound once round the neck with the ends hanging loose

female.outfit: Soft wool twinset (short-sleeved jumper with a matching cardigan) in a pastel or heather tone, tucked into a below-the-knee A-line tweed skirt. Seamed stockings and low-heeled court shoes.
female.hair: Early-1950s 'set': collar-length hair in soft rolled pin-curls framing the face
female.headwear: Printed silk square headscarf folded into a triangle and knotted under the chin, covering the ears, with a roll of curls showing at the forehead; face fully visible
female.accessory: A single strand of pearls (the 'twinset and pearls')

entries.signature: Tweed and knitwear. Men wear an elbow-patched herringbone tweed jacket over a Fair Isle pullover with a flat cap. Women wear a twinset and pearls with a tweed skirt and an under-the-chin headscarf.
avoid: military, Home Guard, ARP or any uniform
Union Jack, royal regalia, guards' bearskins, police helmets
1960s Mod or 1970s punk looks (the wrong moment)
cloche hat, Bubikopf bob or Bauhaus colour-block prints (Germany modern)
broad-brimmed soft felt hat with round wire spectacles and a walrus moustache (Germany modern)
tall-crowned navy peaked cap (China modern)
kerchief knotted at the back of the head with a flower-trimmed edge (Egypt modern)
a likeness of Alan Turing
Sherlock-style deerstalker cliche
entries.notes: Sources: British clothing under rationing and utility schemes around 1946-52, Fair Isle knitwear (Shetland, popular from the 1920s onward), and period photographs of Manchester University computing staff and of northern workers in flat caps. Turing studied at King's College, Cambridge, which inspired the college scarf. The flat cap fits the Manchester and labour theme, though an academic would often have gone bareheaded. Why this moment: Turing c. 1950 was chosen over Pankhurst c. 1910 because it lines up with the computing theme and keeps Britain's modern moment 25 years away from Germany's (1926). RESOLVED: the under-chin headscarf is now Britain-only in this era, because Italy's was removed. Egypt's mandil is also a triangular kerchief, but it is knotted at the nape and edged with crocheted flowers, so keep Britain's knot clearly under the chin. The scarf is now specified as bold block stripes so it cannot be confused with Egypt's plain fringed shal. Pearls are now Britain-only because Iraq's strand was replaced.

entries.moment: Berlin c. 1926, the Weimar Republic's golden age of science and design: Einstein directs the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Physics, and the Bauhaus has just moved to Dessau

male.outfit: Loose, slightly rumpled charcoal three-piece wool suit with wide trousers, a white shirt with a soft turn-down collar and a dark knitted tie. A long dark wool overcoat is worn open.
male.hair: Collar-length hair brushed back from the forehead, a little untidy (not a wild halo)
male.facialHair: Bushy walrus moustache
male.headwear: Broad-brimmed soft black felt hat with a pinched crown
male.accessory: Round wire-rimmed spectacles

female.outfit: Straight, loose, knee-length drop-waist dress with a Bauhaus-style geometric pattern of colour blocks (red, ochre, blue and black squares, bars and circles), worn with flat bar-strap shoes.
female.hair: Bubikopf: a sleek chin-length bob with a blunt fringe
female.headwear: Close-fitting felt cloche hat pulled down to the eyebrows, with a small brim so the face stays clear
female.accessory: Geometric chrome-and-brass necklace of circles and bars in the Bauhaus metal-workshop style

entries.signature: For women, Bauhaus colour-block geometry with a Bubikopf bob and cloche. For men, a broad-brimmed soft felt hat, walrus moustache and round wire spectacles.
avoid: ANY uniform, armband, swastika or other regime or military insignia
brown shirts, black shirts, jackboots, leather trench coats (secret-police stereotype)
Iron Cross, eagles, black-white-red imperial colours
toothbrush moustache
monocle or Pickelhaube
lederhosen, dirndl or beer-hall caricature
'Cabaret' decadence caricature (fishnets, lingerie)
a likeness of Einstein (no wild white hair, no famous-portrait pose)
tweed flat cap, Fair Isle knitwear or twinset and pearls (Britain modern)
entries.notes: Sources: period photographs of Einstein in Berlin (1917-1932) for the rumpled suit, soft collar and moustache. Bauhaus weaving workshop (Gunta Stoelzl, Anni Albers) for the colour-block textiles. Naum Slutzky's geometric chrome-plated brass jewellery (his best-known necklace dates from c. 1929, a few years after the moment). Bubikopf is the German term for the 1920s bob. Why this moment: Weimar 1926 was chosen deliberately over Sophie Scholl (Munich 1942-43) so the look stays fully clear of 1933-45 regime imagery. It was also chosen over Haber (Karlsruhe 1909), which would repeat the Wilhelmine look. CHANGED: the man's hair was toned down, and 'no Einstein likeness' was added, because unruly swept-back hair plus a bushy moustache is the Einstein caricature. Uncertain: the Bauhaus colour-block dress is a stylisation, because Bauhaus weaving mostly made furnishing fabrics and similar 'simultaneous' dresses came from Sonia Delaunay in Paris. The cloche and bob were international 1920s fashions. Within this era Germany is safe because it is the only 1920s entry (all the others are 1950-1980), so the drop waist, cloche and brimmed felt hat are unique.

futureMotifs.motifs: Crisp white and ecru knife-pleated linen; concentric broad-collar necklines reworked as layered circular yokes in bead-row colours (Nile turquoise, lapis blue, carnelian red, gold); kohl-wing graphic lines as piping along seams; vertical fluting taken from lotus and papyrus columns; Mamluk oversized hanging sleeves as dramatic cape-sleeves; the tarboush's truncated cone as a sleek crimson cap with a single tassel; mashrabiya lattice perforation and irrigation-canal grid quilting. Avoid god emblems, royal crowns and cobra motifs.

Tiered Babylonian fringe as kinetic hem and shoulder fringing; one-shoulder spiral draping; embossed cuneiform-wedge texture and cylinder-seal roll-print bands (decorative, not readable); glazed-brick lapis blue with ochre, date-palm brown, cream and gold; the Abbasid tall-cap silhouette and taylasan shoulder shawl as a high hood-collar; tiraz armbands in pseudo-script; square-shouldered open 'aba cloaks with gold-thread yoke edging; the concentric circles of Baghdad's Round City and muqarnas honeycomb geometry; flowing parametric curves recalling Iraqi-born Zaha Hadid's architecture; the sidara's folded boat-shaped crown. Avoid religious text and deity motifs.

Meander (Greek key) and wave-scroll borders as glowing trim lines on hems and cuffs. Asymmetric one-shoulder drapes from the himation and chiton, and crisp accordion pleating from the fustanella. Round fibula-style shoulder clasps, and Byzantine gold roundel (segmenta) inserts as circular panels. Palette of chalk white, Aegean blue, terracotta and black from red-figure pottery, with fine olive-leaf line embroidery. Striped hand-woven crossbody bags echoing the tagari, and tall brimmed crown shapes echoing the Palaiologan hat.

Sweeping curved toga-like wraps with slim vertical clavi-stripe accents. Renaissance slashed-and-puffed sleeves with contrasting linings, and pomegranate damask/velvet patterns rendered as cut or iridescent textures. Palette of Florentine crimson, ochre, terracotta, travertine and Carrara-marble veining. Circular tabarro capes with velvet collars, razor-slim 1960s Roman tailoring with dark visor lenses, and kaleidoscopic swirl prints. A thin lenza forehead band reimagined as a light strip, with Vitruvian circle-and-square geometry, arcade arches and Marconi-style concentric radio-wave rings as graphic motifs.

Diagonal cross-collar (jiaoling) wrap closures and high standing collars fastened with sculpted pankou knot buttons. Deep, flowing sleeves cut as sheer layered panels. Horse-face (mamian) pleated side panels on long coats and skirts. Cloud-scroll (xiangyun) and key-fret (huiwen) borders reworked as glowing circuit-trace trim. Paper-fold pleating and translucent layers like xuan paper pages. Movable-type grids and star-chart or compass-rose line engraving for the navigation and knowledge theme. Jade-like translucent fastenings and lacquer finishes. Palette: ink black, cinnabar lacquer red, celadon, indigo, gold-thread accents. No imperial five-claw dragons, rank squares, flags or political badges.

Kimono collar layering (kasane colour stacking) as a signature neckline. Wide, structured obi-style waist cinchers with modular clasps and obijime cord detail. Clean architectural shoulder lines inspired by the haori and kataginu. Hakama pleat geometry in wide trousers and skirts. Precise geometric patterns (asanoha hemp leaf, seigaiha waves, shippo, kikko, yagasuri) rendered as laser-cut or LED line work. Sashiko grid stitching and origami-fold panels. Visible karakuri-style mechanical joints and split-toe tabi footwear. Palette: aizome indigo, sumi black, washi white, vermilion lacquer, Hokusai Prussian blue, soft sakura-pink accents. No rising-sun rays, imperial chrysanthemum, flags or military insignia.

Sharp Savile Row-style tailoring stretched into long frock-coat lines with high stand collars. Herringbone tweed, Fair Isle knit bands and bold Iron Age checks re-rendered as fine woven or circuit-trace micro-patterns. An open neck ring inspired by the torc. Pleated translucent collar rings that echo the Elizabethan ruff. Paisley teardrop scrollwork etched into panels. Brass rivets, railway-line pinstripes and punch-card perforation grids that recall steam, the telegraph and the computing of Lovelace and Turing. Palette: racing green, oxblood, slate grey, heather and navy, with brass and copper accents.

Bauhaus geometry (circle, square, triangle) in red, yellow, blue and black on graphite. Clean, precision-engineered seams and round lens-like visor or spectacle elements that recall Jena optics. Jugendstil 'whiplash' curves as embroidered or laser-cut trim. Renaissance slashing and puffing reinterpreted as vented panels with contrasting linings. A wide, flat, soft Barett-style cap. Frilled, Kruseler-like pleated collars framing the face. Movable-type grid texture (letterforms used as pattern, never as slogans). Baltic amber and linen-white accents. Avoid black-white-red combinations, eagles, crosses and blackletter lettering.

changes: Italy: the U-shaped sinus fold and umbo pouch were anachronistic for 50 BCE. The sinus is late 1st century BCE–Augustan and the umbo appears around the Ara Pacis, 9 BCE (Rothfus 2010, after Goette 1990). The toga is now drawn the late-Republican way: long single layer, rounded curved edge, firm diagonal band across the chest. The signature is now the curved-edged plain white toga with clavus, clean-shaven face and calcei, plus the nodus for women. The deep sinus and umbo, the broad stripe and the toga sling were added to avoid, and the notes were corrected (the Ara Pacis is not a valid model).

Greece: the petasos moved from 'hanging behind the shoulders' (invisible on a front-facing figure and a halo risk) to headwear worn tilted back with the face clear. The accessory became a pera shoulder pouch, so the Greek accessory no longer collides with the Roman ring. The woman's girdle moved from under the bust (Hellenistic) to the natural waist (Classical). 'Krepides' was replaced with simple strapped sandals. Avoid now also lists the ephebe chlamys-plus-petasos costume and the high girdle.

Iraq: the woman's 'several layered bands of fringe' drifted toward the tiered flounced robe that marks goddesses in Old Babylonian art (a sacred-dress risk), so it is now a single fringed wrap and flounced robes are in avoid. The man's beard changed from strict horizontal rows of tight curls (Neo-Assyrian) to long wavy strands ending in curls. 'Indigo/saffron' became generic red, blue or yellow dye, noted as uncertain.

Egypt: fixed the wrong term 'short-sleeved' wig to a shoulder-length bobbed official's wig. Removed the knotted sheer shawl from the woman, because sheer pleated overgarments came later in the 18th dynasty. Simplified the kilt (the stiff triangular apron is more Middle Kingdom). Added later-18th-dynasty fashion and perfume cones to avoid, and noted that Menna TT69 is c. 1400 BCE, so Rekhmire is the closer model.

China: the jieze had no chin ties (those belong to the formal guan worn over it). It is now a forehead band with a roof ridge and two upright back 'ears'. Confirmed that women's quju robes persisted into Eastern Han, so the woman's spiral hem stays. Added the jinxian guan and seal ribbons (rank markers) and chin ties to avoid.

Japan: corrected the date of the right-lapel rule from the '718 Yoro Code' to the 719 edict (Shoku Nihongi, Yoro 3). Haniwa show the closure in both directions before it, so closure direction was dropped as a tell and the jacket is now fastened with bows at the chest, as haniwa show. Removed the confusing 'left-over-right' avoid item and added 'Chinese big-sleeved robes' and an imperial-regalia-style single jewel to avoid.

Germany: removed the fur-edged collar (caricature drift; Thorsberg shows fringed wool). Removed the woman's sprang hairnet (weakly attested for 1st-century Germania, and a thumbnail duplicate of the Greek sakkos); she now has a woven hair-band (Huldremose) and headwear 'none'. The woman's dress is now a loose peplos-type dress pinned at both shoulders, to separate it from the Egyptian sleeveless sheath. Added the Egypt sheath, snood/hairnet and fur to avoid.
Britain: no substantive changes (checked against Caesar BG 5.14, Dio 62.2 and Diodorus 5.30). Added 'plain undyed cloth with amber' to avoid to protect the distinction from Germany.

EGYPT (sensitivity + accuracy): Mamluk sources say women's izars were white for Muslim women, and blue, yellow and red were the colours imposed on Christian, Jewish and Samaritan women. The izar is now explicitly white and those colours are on the avoid list. The izar hangs open at the front so the coloured gown shows. I removed the unverified claim that sultans decreed shorter sleeves; the only decrees I found (1426/7, 1472) are about women's caps. The man's outer robe changed from indigo to green/brown/dark blue and loses its tiraz bands, so it is not the same as Abbasid Iraq. The men's sleeves are moderated from knee-length to 'well past the fingertips'. The woman's pearl necklace became a filigree collar so it does not duplicate Iraq's pearl choker.

GREECE (distinctiveness + accuracy): the woman's white headcloth wound round the head and neck was nearly identical at thumbnail size to Britain's headrail and Egypt's white izar. It is now a compact, patterned cream/gold/red wound turban (fakiolion) with the neck open and big crescent earrings. The bell-sleeved gown (which echoed Britain) became the fitted, sleeveless, flared silk damask over-dress excavated at Mystras (15th c.), worn over a long-sleeved patterned under-tunic. Men: I dropped the hanging-sleeve overcoat because it hid the button-front tell and echoed Egypt's sleeves. The plaque belt became a belt with small gilt mounts, as attested by Parani. The skaranikon, which bears the emperor's portrait, is added to avoid as regime insignia.

ITALY (distinctiveness + accuracy): the woman's thin white veil was one of five pale female head coverings, and her floor-trailing fur sleeves duplicated Egypt's signature. She now wears the ghirlanda, the Italian padded roll documented for the 1440s, studded with pearls over bare, drawn-back hair and a plucked forehead. Her dress is a gamurra under a sleeveless, open-sided pomegranate-velvet giornea (FIT 1440-49). The man's 'cioppa/lucco with large open sleeves' is clarified as the Florentine lucco. I dropped 'nape shaved high' (a Burgundian/English trait) and state that the mazzocchio sits on top of the head, so it is not read as Germany's Gugel hood.

BRITAIN (distinctiveness): the headrail is now explicitly coloured (blue, brown-red or ochre), as late Anglo-Saxon manuscripts show, and a white headrail is on the avoid list. Its wrap round the throat is the shape tell against Greece's open-necked turban and Egypt's full-length izar. The woman's brooch is now a small gilt one, and the note flags that the Fuller and Pentney brooches are 9th-century references.

GERMANY: the man's gown moved from red to blue/green so it does not echo the red Florentine lucco. The shoes are moderated to 'moderately long', since extreme poulaines peaked around 1460-80. I removed the misapplied 'Kotte' label from the high-belted 1440s gown. The Kruseler's 1440 date is kept, with a source (bloshka: the Wulsthaube evolved from the Kruseler only after c. 1450). Avoid now adds the Italian mazzocchio and ghirlanda.

IRAQ: kept essentially intact. The cap is now specified as stiff, smooth and upright, so it cannot read as Japan's soft black eboshi, and the sleeves end at the wrist so they do not echo Egypt. Avoid now adds Egypt's round all-white turban and white izar.

CHINA: a coloured robe is the official round-collared robe (yuanling pao); the Song lanshan was the pale scholar-student robe. Its colour is set to the mid-rank green or blue-grey, not the purple or vermilion of high ranks. The jade belt plaques (a high-rank marker) became horn or silver, and jade rank belts are added to avoid.

JAPAN: the momi-eboshi is soft and lightly lacquered, since stiff lacquered caps are the tate-eboshi. 'Commoner's hemp suo' conflated two garments and became 'hitatare of hemp', with no family crests. The left-over-right collar is stated explicitly. Avoid now adds a stiff upright cap with a turban base, which reads as Iraq.

Germany male: gave him a full, short-trimmed beard and the shorter 1520s Kolbe haircut, and moved the moment from c. 1520 to c. 1525. Evidence: Duerer's 1526 Holzschuher portrait and the 1520s beard fashion. Why: the old version (clean-shaven, chin-length bob with a fringe, cap, knee-length coat) was nearly the same figure as Italy's Leonardo-era man at thumbnail size, which is the German/Italian doublet clash the brief warned about.

Germany moment: 'Henlein's early pocket watches' became 'early portable spring-driven clocks', because the pocket-watch attribution is disputed. Added the Nuremberg Reformation (1525) as the anchor for the new year.

Italy male: removed the shoulder cloak because it duplicated Britain's man. Fixed 'pitocco/giornea' to 'pitocco', which is the Anonimo Gaddiano's word; a giornea is a different, open-sided garment. Made the berretta explicitly small, round and red, after Leonardo's Portrait of a Musician. Added avoid-rules that ban a beard, the Barett, the Schaube and gold chains.

Italy female: added a small central brow jewel to the lenza (as in La Belle Ferronniere) so the hair-thin cord reads at thumbnail size, and stated she wears no hat, to separate her from Germany's Barett-wearing woman.

Japan male: replaced 'stiff broad shoulders that flare out like wings' with modest, flat, squared shoulders. Japanese costume histories say the widening came during the Edo period and whale-baleen stiffening around the Genroku era (1688-1703), so winged shoulders were anachronistic for 1610. Removed crests entirely (no real or generic mon). Moved the thumbnail tell onto the sleeveless vest, the hakama and the bareheaded shaved-pate topknot. Added winged shoulders to the avoid list and a kinchaku pouch as a fallback if the inro is too early.

China female: lengthened the ao from hip to knee length and made it front-opening, per late-Ming paintings and Tiangong Kaiwu. Changed the skirt from deep red or green to plain white or pale, per the Chongzhen-era fashion. Swapped the jinbu knee-length jade-and-tassel pendant for gold gourd earrings, because the pendant duplicated Japan's tasselled Nagoya-obi. Renamed the forehead band 'baotou (tougu)' and specified that it is broad, to set it apart from Italy's hair-thin lenza.

China male: changed 'long drooping moustache and long thin chin beard' to a neatly trimmed moustache and a neat chin beard, to avoid the Fu Manchu caricature (sensitivity). Dropped white from the robe colours (white reads as mourning). Specified that the cap is box-like with visible corners, and added avoid-rules against fur caps and dark fur-edged coats, to stay apart from Greece.

Greece male: specified a brimless, fur-textured kalpak with a rounded top. This keeps it apart from China's square gauze cap and avoids the mitre-shaped variant, which reads as clergy. Changed the fur to fox or lamb and the sash to silk-cotton, since Ottoman rules restricted sable and luxury silk for Christians. Added the 1662 ban on red kalpaks to the avoid list. Removed 'dark' from 'full dark beard', because hair colour must never be a tell.

Egypt: backed the female tartur with Cornelis de Bruyn's 1698 eyewitness description (tall hat wrapped in black or brown cloth with gold or silver stripes). The description now says it widens toward the top and the veil hangs down the back. Changed the fallback so it no longer uses a red cap with a kerchief, which would collide with Greece's woman. Made the male turban explicitly pure white. Softened the Kashmir shawl to 'Kashmir or Indian shawl' and flagged it as plausible, not certain, for 1700.

Iraq: corrected the moment. Baghdad was under Hasan Pasha (1704-23), whose household later became the Mamluk regime; Mamluk pashas ruled in their own right only from 1747. Made the turban explicitly coloured, never white. Clarified that the 'aba has arm slits. Replaced the crescents in the qilada necklace with coins and teardrops, to avoid any reading as a later Ottoman state emblem. Flagged the turban pattern as the least-attested detail.

Britain: accuracy unchanged. Updated the avoid list's Germany reference to c. 1525 and added gold chains and the Barett as German tells to avoid. Noted that the pearl earring is more courtly than mercantile but still plausible.

Men: white turban with a red top (Egypt), coloured turban with a striped 'aba (Iraq), rounded black fur kalpak with a fur-edged coat (Greece), small red cap with a bob and a pink knee gown (Italy), square black gauze cap with a pale wide-sleeved robe (China), bareheaded topknot with a sleeveless vest and hakama (Japan), ruff with a tall brimmed hat (Britain), wide tilted Barett with a beard and fur collar (Germany). Women: tartur (Egypt), black head-shawl with a brow band and dark cloak (Iraq), red cap with a scarf and silver pafti (Greece), hatless hair with a jewelled lenza and white sleeve puffs (Italy), long standing-collar jacket over a horse-face skirt (China), dark patterned kosode with a tasselled cord belt (Japan), ruff with a tall hat over a coif (Britain), tilted Barett with the Goller cape (Germany). No country was missing.
Egypt: moved the date from 1865 to 1869. The title 'Khedive' was granted by firman on 8 June 1867, so 'Khedivate of Egypt' in 1865 was anachronistic.

Egypt (women): the visible headwear is now Lane's long white embroidered tarha veil trailing down the back, replacing the red tarboush with gold kurs. The kurs is documented c. 1835 and uncertain for 1869, and a small red cap was confusable with the Greek women's red fesi. The women's signature was updated to match.
Egypt (men): the tarboush is now described as stiff, upright, level, with a short tassel, to separate it from the Greek fesi, which is floppy and tilted with a long tassel.

Iraq (men): the headcloth is now plain white, to avoid chequered patterns with modern political associations. The 'aba is now camel-brown, so it cannot be read as Italy's black tabarro and differs from the woman's black 'abaya. The signet ring, which is invisible at thumbnail size, was replaced by a brass dawat pen-case tucked into the girdle.
Iraq: the notes now state honestly that the headcloth with 'igal was one of several Baghdad townsman looks (with turbans and the fez), chosen for distinctiveness.

Greece: jackets changed to crimson (men) and burgundy (women) with an ivory or rose skirt, so the look avoids a blue-and-white flag scheme. The fesi is described as soft and drooping. The women's signature now leads with the gold-embroidered kontogouni, not only the red cap. Checked against Amalia-costume sources: red fesi with a long braided-gold tassel worn at an angle, and a short gold-embroidered velvet jacket.

Italy: the lobbia (dented crown, medium brim) was replaced by a broad-brimmed soft black felt hat, because the lobbia is almost identical to Germany's Homburg at thumbnail size. The moustache is now bushy 'Umbertine' rather than curled, to separate it from Germany's waxed style. Added a note that by 1895 the tabarro was more provincial or old-fashioned.

China (men): removed the long, thin, drooping moustache, which is effectively the banned 'Fu Manchu' look; he is now clean-shaven, as Qing custom was. The round spectacles were replaced by a hebao purse at the hip to avoid overlap with Germany's pince-nez.

China (women): added a black embroidered meile forehead band as a thumbnail tell; it was worn by Qing women of all ranks. Removed the short fringe, which is more 1890s-1900s and would sit under the band.

Japan (men): replaced the pocket-watch chain, which duplicated Egypt and Britain, with the white haori-himo cord knot. The moustache is now straight, not upturned. Footwear reduced to a single choice. Added a note that the kimono collar crosses left over right, with an avoid item explaining why.
Japan (women): flagged that hair ribbons and women's hakama are at the early edge for 1899 (mostly c. 1900-05).
Britain: the moment text claimed 1843 was 'the height of Railway Mania', but the mania peaked in 1845-47, so it now says 'just before' and mentions the Cooke-Wheatstone telegraph.

Germany: toned the 'Es ist erreicht' moustache down to a moderate twist to avoid the stern-Prussian caricature when combined with the brush cut and pince-nez, and added exaggerated Kaiser points to the avoid list.

All entries: added cross-country avoid items (Egypt/Greece fez, Egypt/Iraq head coverings, Italy/Germany hats, Italy/Britain shawls, Japan/Germany bowler) so the image model does not blur neighbouring looks.

Bouffant/sunglasses, the melaya laff (reads as Iraq's 'abaya) and belly-dance caricature were added to the avoid list.

China male: the cap's shape is now spelled out (tall rounded stiffened crown, sitting high, no badge) to separate it from Britain's low tweed flat cap. The satchel is specified as plain and unstriped to separate it from Greece's tagari.

Britain: the scarf is now specified as broad block stripes, and the headscarf knot clearly under the chin, to separate them from Egypt's plain shal and nape-knotted mandil. 'A likeness of Alan Turing' and the China and Egypt look-alikes were added to the avoid list. Britain now owns the under-chin headscarf and the pearls alone in this era.

All eight countries were already present. No sensitivity breaches were found beyond the caricature risks above. Every head covering is described with the face fully visible.
confusable: Italy male vs Greece male: the late-Republican toga (c. 50 BCE) is itself a himation-like drape, so the silhouettes are close. The difference rests on the clean-shaven face, plain white curved-edge toga, visible purple clavus and calcei (Rome) against the beard, coloured meander-bordered himation, petasos and pera (Greece). Moving Rome to the Augustan era (c. 10 CE) would restore the unmistakable sinus and umbo, if the Caesar moment is not required.

Italy female vs Greece female: both wear a long dress under a draped mantle. The tell is the headwear or hair (Greek sakkos snood against the Roman nodus roll) plus the Greek meander hem against the plain palla and visible stola straps.

Greece male vs Iraq male: both are bearded men in a coloured mantle over the left shoulder. The tell is the Babylonian chest-length curled beard, nape bun, headband and heavy fringe against the Greek short beard, short curls, petasos and woven border.

Britain male vs Germany male: they share the tunic, trousers and shoulder-pinned cloak silhouette. The difference rests on the multicoloured checks, gold torc and moustache-only face (Britain) against plain brown or blue twill, the Suebian side knot and a full beard (Germany).

Egypt female vs Germany female: both wear sleeveless ankle-length linen dresses. The difference rests on the heavy tripartite wig, broad bead collar and fitted white sheath (Egypt) against the nape knot, loose shoulder-pinned dress with red trim, wool shawl and amber beads (Germany).

iraq male vs japan male: both wear tall black caps. They must be drawn differently: Iraq's cap is stiff, smooth and upright, rising out of a white turban band, with tiraz armbands; Japan's is soft, crumpled and forward-leaning, with no turban, and wide square hitatare sleeves with hakama.
iraq male vs greece male: both are bearded men in tall hats and long robes. The tells are the white turban at the base of Iraq's black cone against Greece's turned-up brim and button-front robe.

italy male vs germany male: both are clean-shaven, in pleated gowns, with hood-derived headwear that has a tail. Italy wears a padded ring sitting on top of the head, visible hair and an ankle-length red lucco. Germany wears a hood enclosing the head and neck with a scalloped shoulder cape, a calf-length blue or green Tappert and pointed shoes. Artists must not merge the two.

egypt female vs britain female: both drape the head and shoulders. They differ in colour and shape: Egypt's white izar hangs open to the ankles over a bright gown, while Britain's coloured headrail wraps round the throat and ends at the back. The difference relies partly on garment colour, so the shapes must be exaggerated.

greece female vs italy female: both have a rounded volume on the head. Greece's is a tall wound turban covering all the hair, with crescent earrings. Italy's is a padded pearl-studded ring with bare hair and a high forehead showing inside and below it.

China male vs Greece male: both wear a tall black cap over an ankle-length robe. Mitigated by making China's cap square and box-like in stiff gauze over a pale, very wide-sleeved robe with a white collar strip, and Greece's a rounded, fur-textured kalpak over a dark, fur-edged coat. Needs checking at thumbnail after generation.

Egypt male vs Iraq male: both are bearded, turbaned men in long robes. The tell depends on Egypt's turban staying pure white with the red crown visible, and on Iraq's coloured, patterned turban plus the broad brown-and-cream striped 'aba. If the image model whitens Iraq's turban or drops the 'aba stripes, the two merge.

Italy female vs Germany female: both gowns show white puffs at the sleeves. The German Barett and black Goller cape against the hatless Italian with a jewelled lenza carry the difference; the German woman must never lose her hat.

Forehead bands on three women (Iraq's black 'asaba over a head-shawl, Italy's hair-thin lenza with a jewel, China's broad black baotou under a high bun): each is set apart by its context, but none of them should be used as that country's sole tell.

Egypt men (stiff upright crimson tarboush) vs Greece men (soft, drooping red fesi): both are red fez-type caps. The full outfits are distinct (black stambouline vs white fustanella), but a leaked cap alone could be rendered alike. The image prompts must enforce stiff/level/short tassel vs floppy/tilted/long tassel.

Japan men (bowler) vs Germany men (Homburg): both are dark Western felt hats. Tell them apart by the haori, himo cord and striped hakama vs the frock coat, tall collar and pince-nez, and by the bowler's round dome vs the Homburg's dented crown and curled brim.

Italy women (black fringed scialle) vs Britain women (Paisley shawl): both drape a shawl over a long dress. The tells are Britain's poke bonnet and bell skirt with ringlets vs Italy's bare high chignon and red coral necklace.

Egypt, Britain and Germany men all wear dark frock coats, and Egypt and Britain both wear a gold watch chain. The coats alone do not separate them; the headwear (tarboush, top hat, Homburg) must always be drawn clearly.
Greece, Italy and Germany men all wear full moustaches with shaped ends. Facial hair should not be relied on as a tell in this era.

Italy male vs Japan male: near-identical slim dark suits and bare heads. Rome depends on the solid black sunglasses; Tokyo depends on the orange-foam headphones and the lapel badge. Both must always be drawn.

China male cap vs Britain male flat cap: both are soft peaked caps. They are only separable by the tall, high-sitting navy crown versus the low, sloping brown tweed crown, so the illustrator must keep the silhouettes distinct.

Egypt female mandil vs Britain female headscarf: both are triangular kerchiefs. They differ in knot position (nape versus under the chin) and in Egypt's crocheted-flower edge, which may blur at thumbnail size.
China female khaki satchel vs Greece tagari: both are crossbody bags. They differ only in the plain khaki versus bold stripes and fringe.
Egypt male shal vs Britain male college scarf: both are long wool neck scarves. Plain dark with a fringe versus bold block stripes should hold, but only if the stripes are drawn strongly.
Iraq male horn-rims vs Germany male round wire spectacles: both are clear-lens glasses. Heavy black rectangular frames versus thin round wire frames are only separable if drawn at sufficient size.
Egypt female gold bangles vs Iraq female gold coin pendant: both are gold jewellery, told apart only by placement (wrists versus neckline).
